PREFACE

Business history, administrative history, and social history are three
relatively recent additions to the general field of history. All reflect
a new sense of values and all are dependent upon new sources of
information.

In the Baker Library, Harvard University, there has been deposited,
through the generosity of Mr H. Gordon Selfridge, of London, Eng-
land, a valuable collection of business records kept by the Medici
family of Florence. The scholar at all familar with the mediaeval
field has no difficulty in using these documents in a general and super-
ficial manner. Exact transcription and translation, however, have been
difficult and in places impossible. The present Glossary has been
compiled by Dr Florence Edler in order to aid students who wish to
use these and other similar records.

A larger number of citations has been furnished by M. Robert
Brun, of the Bibliothéque Nationale. A smaller number has come
from Professor Armando Sapori, of Florence, Italy, who has been
prevented by circumstances from completing his task.

Another collaborator in the work is Dr Allan Evans, who will in
the near future prepare a separate treatise on Italian coins, especially
those in use about 1340, the date of Pegolotti’s treatise which is the
starting point of his studies. Professor Eugene H. Byrne, of Barnard
College, is directing an additional part of the undertaking, namely a
Latin series of terms of business used in mediaeval Genoa, to be pub-
lished later. Working with Professor Byrne are Professor Robert L.
Reynolds and Dr Hilmar Krueger, of the University of Wisconsin.

The particular objectives of Dr Edler are clearly set forth in her
introduction. A central part of the plan, and one upon which the
work must be judged, is that not only should the meaning of words
and terms be elucidated but the citations should be long enough to be of
value to economic and business historians. It is this dual objective
that has made the Glossary sui generis.

Light is thrown upon partnership, management, accounting, and
marketing, so important to the business historian. Information is
provided on the subject of the organization of manufacture and the
direction of foreign trade, somewhat more emphasized by the economic
historian.

vii

viii PREFACE

A special advisory committee has given valuable assistance during
the progress of the work. The committee consists of Professor Walter
L. Bullock, University of Chicago, Professor Edwin F. Gay, Harvard
University, and Professor A. A. Vasiliev, University of Wisconsin.
To each of them our best thanks!

Thus it is obvious that the present enterprise has been cooperative.
But there has been even more cooperation—institutional. The Me-
diaeval Academy of America has sponsored the undertaking and has
guided its course throughout. Indeed this volume is the first of the
Academy’s cooperative projects to appear in print. The Harvard
Graduate School of Business Administration has provided accommoda-
tion and other assistance from first to last. The American Council
of Learned Societies has generously financed the research which could
hardly have been undertaken otherwise.

N.S. B. Gras

HARVARD UNIVERSITY Director of the Project

INTRODUCTION

AIM AND SCOPE OF THE GLOSSARY

Every student of economic history who has had occasion to use
the wealth of published and unpublished Italian economic sources of the
thirteenth, fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth centuries has been
faced with the extreme difficulty of interpreting such documents.
This has been partly owing to palaeographical difficulties in manuscripts
and to linguistic problems in both manuscript and printed sources.
Most of the published documents are unedited, or at best poorly done.
Recently, however, a number of Italian scholars, such as Bensa, Ciasca,
Chiaudano, Lazzareschi, Sapori, and others, have undertaken the
publication of admirably edited sources; but innumerable previously
published volumes of source material for business history are almost
unusable by the scholar who has neither the time nor the facilities to
work out the meaning of each term in a given document.

Very few of the edited sources contain glossaries of value. With
one or two exceptions, the dictionaries are of little assistance. The
well-known Crusca dictionary, in its effort to standardize modern
Italian, has omitted obsolete words and many obsolete meanings of
words in current use. Other dictionaries, such as Hoare, Italian
Dictionary, Petrocchi, Novo dizionario universale, and Tommaseo and
Bellini, Dizionario della lingua italiana, do list many obsolete words,
but from their very nature as dictionaries they present definitions
which are frequently too comprehensive to explain the meanings pecu-
liar to specific business usage. The number of business terms found
in the dialectal dictionaries is very limited. Rezasco’s Dizionario
della lingua storica e amministrativa is invaluable to the worker in
political, economic, and social history, but it excludes the large classes
of words dealing with industry and commerce, coins, and weights and
measures, and includes but few terms of banking and accounting.

Although modern historiography has been rather barren in so
far as new types of source material are concerned, a new and relatively
untapped source remains in the form of business records. Material
of this nature, though but poorly preserved for most countries, exists
in large quantities for Italian as for American history. Its great value
is now being fully realized by a few scholars, but much pioneering
work remains to be done. My aim has been to facilitate research

ix

x INTRODUCTION

in this type of material, and to prepare a work which would in some
measure supply the need for a manual or reference book, so strongly felt
by the student of mediaeval Italian economic documents.

While the needs of the economic historian have been foremost in
mind, the student of social and cultural history and of literature may
profit by some of the material which is included herein. Scholars
have found the literature of the period covered by the Glossary, 1200-
1600—especially English and Italian literature—full of commercial
terms and ideas. Just as students of Chaucer have found that much
in his work can be understood only with the aid of precise definitions of
business terms, as they were used in the England of his day, so the
explanation of much in the works of Italian writers, especially the
novellisti, Boccaccio, Sacchetti, and others, requires a knowledge of
Italian business terms, a knowledge of the “slang of the market-place.”
The large number of diaries, personal journals, ‘‘secret books,’ letters,
etc., from which citations have been taken (see the List of Abbrevia-
tions of Sources in this work) may give some idea of the part that
business terms play in the semi-literary works of the period. Many
letters and journals of mediaeval business men have been published
unedited because no glossary or dictionary was at hand to explain the
business terms found in them. For the benefit of the student of
cultural history, some terms, which might otherwise have been omit-
ted, have been included, for example, a(no)ne avuto, a(no)ne dato.
These would not puzzle an historian who was actually handling busi-
ness sources, such as account books where the meaning of the phrases,
appearing on almost every page, is obvious; but when they occur in
literary sources, such as diaries, away from their setting, they cause
difficulties which no existing dictionary can solve.

The guiding principle throughout the compilation of this present
work has therefore been to produce a glossary (and not a dictionary)
of the exact and peculiar usage of such business terms as the economic
historian and the student of social and cultural history is likely to meet
in using Italian sources, both those already familiar and those as yet
unexplored.

In the choice of terms I have had in mind: (1) obsolete words not
found in the standard dictionaries (although possibly in the dialectal
ones); (2) words found in modern Italian but with a changed meaning
or meanings; and (3) interesting terms the meaning of which has not
changed from the Middle Ages to the present, but of which instances
have been found that throw light upon some points in economic history.

Four large groups of terms have been included in this volume:
(1) general business terms which include terms of accounting, banking,

INTRODUCTION xi

and exchange, buying and selling for cash, barter and credit, insurance
and surety, transportation and warehousing, custom dues and tolls, and
forms of business association; (2) terms for artisans and trades and
industrial processes; (3) weights and measures; and (4) commodities.
Coins have been omitted because a separate glossary of mediaeval
Italian coins is being prepared by Dr Allan Evans. For some time it
was planned to keep the terms belonging to each main division together
and have three or four parts within one volume, but the inconvenience
of this method, by which a number of terms would have appeared in
two or three sections, outweighed the slight advantage of being able to
find all the terms for weights and measures, or commodities, within a
few pages.

Little attempt has been made to give the modern equivalents of
weights and measures. Mediaeval weights and measures varied so
greatly that we are unable to establish their exact values. Instead,
the Florentine and Venetian systems have been taken as the standards
in terms of which almost all other measures can be expressed.

Very few terms for commodities appear in this volume. The only
ones included are those for which examples have been found that throw
some light on the exact meaning of the commodity term—principally
in the unpublished Datini and Medici sources. Citations from Pego-
lotti have been little used for commodities because Dr Allan Evans
has prepared an excellent glossary of cloth, spices, etc., to accompany
his new edition and translation of Pegolotti.

The sources used are certain groups of printed documents and
unpublished manuscripts to which I and my collaborators, M. Robert
Brun and Professor Armando Sapori, have had access and which,
fortunately, are widely representative of the kinds of materials with
which future work will be concerned. The date 1200 has been chosen
as an approximate starting point because the oldest extant business
records in Italian date from about that time (or more precisely, from
1211). The terminal date of 1600 has been chosen because the Medici
material extends to approximately that date. The printed material is
of several types—merchant letters and personal diaries and journals,
account books and bookkeeping manuals, partnership agreements, com-
mercial instruments. merchant handbooks, customs records, commercial
treaties, and statutes of gilds and city-states. Most of the published
sources are for northern and central Italy, especially for Tuscany.
Problems of dialect have not caused much trouble. The language of
Italian merchants proved to be more uniform than was anticipated.

The unpublished sources from which citations are given are
chiefly the Datini Archives in Prato, Italy, the Bardi and Peruzzi
xii INTRODUCTION

documents in private and public archives in Florence, and the Selfridge
Collection of Medici Manuscripts on deposit at Harvard University.
Professor Sapori has sent some citations from manuscripts in Siena.
A few examples have been taken from transcriptions I made of docu-
ments in the Florentine and Lucchese archives and in the Cavagna
Collection of Italian Manuscripts in the University of Illinois Library.
Professor Sapori has made a careful study of the Peruzzi account books
in Florence and the Tolomei accounts in Siena. All the citations
from Bardi, Peruzzi, and Tolomei manuscripts are from cards sent by
Professor Sapori, except for a few citations taken from his pub-
lished works on the Bardi and Peruzzi. M. Brun has contributed a
very large number of terms with citations taken from the Datini mer-
cantile letters, and a number from the account books. Some idea of
my indebtedness to him for his collaboration may be obtained from
the large number of examples given with references to the Datini
archives. Whenever the reference, Arch. Dat., etc., is found, the cita-
tion is one supplied by M. Brun. Much of the material provided by
my two collaborators has not been used, but all of it greatly furthered
the work of preparing definitions, even though I sometimes found
other and better examples to cite than those taken from the Datini
records or the Peruzzi or Tolomei account books.

Not all of the Medici Manuscripts in the Selfridge Collection have
been used, but I have taken citations from representative accounts of
the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

Every scholar who examines the Glossary will be able to list
omissions of terms which, in his opinion, should be included. Many
will question some of the definitions in the light of sources with which
they are familiar. Notice of such omissions and such criticism will be
welcomed by the compiler.

This Glossary, which is essentially a pioneering work, is necessarily
incomplete: in some senses it is too limited in scope, in others too broad,
to be well-rounded. The long period covered (from 1200 to 1600)
and the variety of regional sources used (from Sicily to Northern
Italy) have made the task of collecting and sorting material extremely
difficult. Tuscan material predominates, of course, because more of it
is extant in published and unpublished form than for any other part of
Italy.

From the very beginning it was realized that this Glossary would
not be in anything like orthodox form, partly because it is not based on
one source or set of sources, and partly because it has a definite purpose
of selection of one large class of terms, instead of an explanation of all
the unusual terms found in a given source. The inclusion of citations,

INTRODUCTION xiii

many of them long ones, also distinguishes it from most glossaries.
As the work progressed, it became clear that appendices offered the
only solution to the problem of how to give more detailed explanations
and longer citations for terms than could be done in the body of the
Glossary.

The appendices, particularly the longer ones, have shaped them-
selves; their length may seem out of proportion in a work, which, by
its very nature, should be concise. The material included in the
appendices on bookkeeping, credit, and partnerships is important, new
in English at least, and closely related to a large number of terms.
The omission of such material would lessen the usefulness of the Glos-
sary as a tool for students who wish to make use of that new type of
source material—mercantile account books—material which has been
largely neglected because of the great difficulties in the way of inter-
pretation of terms and abbreviations. Since all of the appendices are
based on material in the Selfridge Collection of Medici Manuscripts,
they are not presented as complete treatments of a general subject.

The diagrams for the terms connected with the woolen-cloth
industry, the silk industry, and weights and measures have been worked
# out to clarify the relations of terms within each group. Their useful-

E ness appeared to warrant their inclusion here.

q A great deal of the work which has been done in connection with
a the Glossary has led to no direct result. Many works on commercial
y law, economic thought, philology, and historical works of sundry kinds
di have been consulted. This work has gone into background, selections,
a definitions, and so forth. Certain sources of information have proved
3 disappointing; for example, the Latin treatises on commercial law of the

fifteenth and sixteenth centuries have not yielded the explanation of
certain difficult terms and practices sought for in them. On the other
hand, the gild and municipal statutes, both Latin and Italian, have
Ù proved much more helpful than was anticipated. Difficult abbrevia-
lE tions in some of the industrial account books of the sixteenth century
Bi have been solved by the use of statutory regulations for the woolen
; industry, published by Cantini in his long series of Legislazione toscana.

With very few exceptions no references to secondary sources are
given in connection with the definitions of terms. A short bibliography
of the most useful secondary sources, especially periodical articles,
has been prepared. It follows the list of primary sources.

Two or three facts regarding the period as a whole should perhaps
be emphasized here: one is the widespread use of the partnership
lasting from three to five years in the interior cities of Italy. The
temporary partnership of the maritime cities has been emphasized in

xiv INTRODUCTION

many economic histories to the neglect of the more prolonged form of
partnership, which was equally common in other places. For further
details, see Appendix I, Medici Partnerships. The importance of the
bill of exchange in the fourteenth, fifteen, and sixteenth centuries
can hardly be exaggerated, and the extensive use of credit (see Ap-
pendix III) should be pointed out.

KEy-WoRDS

The key-words have been arranged in exact alphabetical order.
Separation of words and apostrophes has been ignored, so that artefice
comes between arte and arte maggiore, and libro del taglio between
libro (delle) compere and libro de’ tessitori.

Modern spelling has been used for all the key-words which have a
modern form, even when no example of the modern spelling has been
found within the period of the Glossary. For example, ceragrafio will
be found under chiragrafo, although no instance of the latter spelling
has been found in the documents examined. In order to aid the stu-
dent of mediaeval documents who may not recognize at once the rela-
tion between the mediaeval spelling of a word like ceragrafio and its
modern form, cross-references are given to the modern form from the
variants which cannot be easily recognized. In some instances—when
a variant has a very limited geographical range—reference. is given to
the place where it was used.

Although numerous variants are given, many more have been
omitted. The documents of the period are full of innumerable varia-
tions in the spelling of even the most common words, but most of these
variants are easily recognized. Some of them are dialectal, others
may be explained by the historical development of the Italian language,
and still others are individual in character—misspellings, Latinization,
and so forth.

In Tuscany the use of ch and gh for hard c and g and of ci and gi for
the soft sound of c and g before all vowels, the interchange of m and m
before labials, and the historical use of gn for gn account for many
combinations which appear curious to modern eyes—such as cierta,
chonpangnia, chonpangnio, and giente.

K and qu for c are good thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Flor-
entine usage and sometimes appear in later centuries, for example,
chapitale and kapitale.

In Florentine speech and writing of the fifteenth and sixteenth
centuries, 7 was popularly substituted as the first of a double consonant
(cansa for cassa; fanto, fatto; scrinta, scritta; tranta, tratta) and also
before one or two consonants where it did not replace another conso-

INTRODUCTION XV

nant (anpare for apare; ponsto, posto). N is also frequently omitted
where it belongs in the Medici documents (Lorezo for Lorenzo; ricordaza,
ricordanza). V was frequently dropped from forms of the verb avere
(auta for avuta; arà, avrà).

Dialectal differences account for the frequent interchange of 7
and e, e and a, o and win such words as avire for avere; sensaria, senseria;
butega, bottega; instromento, instrumento; for the omission of t from the
ending -tore (folaore, curaore, garzaore, tiraore for folatore, curatore,
etc.); and for such forms as asio for aggio; cavidale, capitale; raxon,
ragione; zornale, giornale.

Latinization explains the use of # before words beginning with a
vowel—such as havere, hora, and hoste; the substitution of ¢ for 2 in
such words as datio for dazio, mercantia for mercanzia; the use of ct for
tt, dc for cc, and pi for tt—lectera equals lettera; adcomandigia, accoman-
digia; scripta, scritta.

The older forms of mercante and mercanzia are frequently found:
mercatante, mercadante; mercatanzia, mercadantia.

The old plural ending -ora derived from the Latin neuter plural is
used frequently: cambiora, luogora, and pegnora.

The feminine ending -trice is seldom used for words which have a
masculine form in -tore. Instead the analogical ending -tora is used
for the feminine: filatora, tessitora. This feminine in -tora is found in
all the Medici documents of both the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

French influence accounts for such a form as guagno for guadagno.

A very common practice was the interchange of single and double
consonants. Examples can be found showing that almost all double
consonants were frequently written as a single consonant: casa equals
cassa, pano, panno. The converse is also true—single consonants are
frequently doubled: channbbio equals cambio, chontto, conto. Doubling
of an initial consonant frequently occurs in the spelling when the word
causing the doubling is joined to the following word, for example,
affiorini, a fiorini; ellaltro, e l'altro.

Etymologies have been omitted from all words except those coming
directly from Arabic, Persian, Turkish, and Byzantine Greek, that is,
Greek words which did not come into Italian through Latin.

Words which do not appear in the large Italian dictionaries, such
as Crusca and Tommaseo, have been marked with an asterisk. Some
of the starred words may be found in specialized dictionaries such as
Rezasco, or in dialectal ones. Others have not been found in any
dictionary.

In a few instances a second modern word closely resembling the
key-word is placed in parentheses after the key-word. This is done

xvi INTRODUCTION

in instances where, although the key-word exists today, its meaning
has changed and the word in parentheses is the related form which has
retained or acquired the old meaning; for example, scontrare (riscon-
trare), scontro (riscontro), montare (ammontare). As these examples
‘show, the difference between the two words is one of prefixes.

Anyone glancing through the lists of key-words will notice a con-
siderable similarity of terms and even the repetition of words, espe-
cially in terms of money exchange, where /ettera, prima lettera, and
prima will all be found. Such variations and relationships are obvious
enough when the related terms are before us in the present form, but
in research we are not so likely to make the connection, to see the rela-
tionship between similar terms at once. Then in some instances, two
similar terms are not surely related, or at least, not synonymous, as one
might guess them to be; for example, libro segreto and libretto segreto.
Since the aim of the Glossary is to bring out the fine distinctions of
meaning, the inclusion of special forms of words and a certain amount
of repetition of similar terms have been necessary.

DEFINITIONS

The definitions are attempts to state as precisely as possible the
meanings peculiar to the terms as used in mediaeval business practices.

The ideal has not been to give a concise dictionary definition, nor to
turn a neat phrase to be used in a translation, but to give as brief a
descriptive statement as possible which will exactly explain what is
meant by each term.

Only those meanings of which examples have been found in avail-
able sources have been given, even though dictionaries, such as that of
Rezasco, may furnish other usages from unavailable sources. In other
words, although many dictionaries have been consulted, and although
my indebtedness to them, particularly to Hoare and Rezasco, will be
patent to anyone acquainted with their contents, no definitions have
been taken from them without careful verification, and no examples
have been directly copied from Rezasco or others, but in each case
from the original printed or manuscript source. Naturally, this
policy has limited the scope of the work. Before we can have a dic-
tionary of business terms, we must have glossaries covering a more or
less limited range of material.

The part of the definition given within parentheses is explanatory
and is meant to furnish additional information, rather than to restrict
the meaning or application. When a term has a limited geographical
range, the places where the word has been found in use or known to be
used, are also given within the explanatory parentheses. The mention

INTRODUCTION xvii

of only one or two cities after a term does not mean that the term was
strictly limited to use in those cities, but that as yet no examples of its
use elsewhere have been found in the documents examined, although
others may be able to furnish numerous examples of the use of a given
term with a peculiar meaning in places other than those mentioned in
the Glossary.

In the explanatory matter within parentheses an artisan is often
referred to as a master workman, a journeyman, a laborer working for
day wages, etc. These classifications are based on information con-
tained in the citations and in other material—especially the Medici
account books—which have been carefully studied. When payment for
work done was made directly to an artisan by an entrepreneur or by a
merchant, it is safe to say that the artisan was a master, i.e., a skilled
workman who had completed his apprenticeship and who legally could
do work for anyone in his own shop or home or outside. The journey-
man stage was not as clearly defined in Italy as in Northern Europe,
but those artisans who had completed their apprenticeship, yet were
working for master artisans instead of doing work for entrepreneurs,
could be called journeymen. Whether a master was remunerated in
the form of day wages, piece wages, or a lump sum for an entire job
depended upon the industry and the town and not upon his status as a
master. When it is fairly certain how a workman was paid in a given
town or region, I have stated that information.

I have used both terms, ‘manufacturer’ and ‘‘entrepreneur,”’
for the industrialists in the textile industries. By the fifteenth century
most of them were entrepreneurs on a large scale—buying the raw
product, giving it out to be worked, and marketing the finished material.

When the appendices contain explanatory matter pertaining to a
given term, a reference is made to the appendix to this work and some-
times to the page where such material is to be found.

Some groups of words have been more difficult than others to
define: in particular, terms of banking, negotiable paper, and book-
keeping. The general tendency is to translate words by finding modern
equivalents, but many mediaeval practices and words expressing them
have no exact modern equivalent. In an attempt to avoid misusing
such modern terms as cheque, single-entry bookkeeping, balance sheet,
and profit and loss statement, circumlocutions have to be resorted to
which are most unsatisfactory to the translator, however clearly they
may explain what the term or termsmeant. My translation of excerpts
from the Medici account books in the several appendices has shown me
how unsatisfactory some of the longer definitions are when we have to
translate an Italian passage into a minimum of English words. But

xviii INTRODUCTION

the convenience of the translator has had to be sacrificed in favor of the
needs of the economic historian and research worker who wants to
know what a term meant within its setting and what its historical
background was, when that can be determined.

Cross-references are given (1) to synonymous terms, e.g., messetio,
cf. sensale, (2) to terms that are not synonymous but closely related,
and (3) to examples of the use of a term found in citations listed under
other key-words and in the appendices. In a few instances, to prevent
duplication of necessarily long quotations, a key-word is given without
an illustrative example, but with a cross-reference to a quotation found
under another word, whether related or unrelated, e.g., taglia, see ac-
comanda.

CITATIONS AND APPENDICES

The examples have been chosen for their pertinence and for
their special interest to economic and business historians. Irrelevant
and verbose phrases and sentences have been omitted to save space
and to make clearer the use of terms. On the other hand, long passages
have been cited occasionally because, in addition to giving the setting
of a term, they illustrate very interesting or unusual mediaeval business
methods, e.g., accomanda, fondacaio. In other words, emphasis has
been put upon source material for mediaeval economic and business
history.

The strict limitation of the Glossary to Italian terms and sources
has made it impossible to give an adequate presentation of the historical
development of many of the terms whose origins are deeply imbedded
in the early Middle Ages and in the mediaeval Latin documents of those
centuries. This is to be regretted, but the task of tracing many words
back to their origins would require many times the number of years
devoted to this present work. In a very few instances a Latin docu-
ment is quoted in a footnote because it admirably supplements or
explains the use of a term, e.g., corriere di pagamento. Some footnotes
contain translations of citations which are especially puzzling and which
required familiarity with similar documents in order to be understood
and interpreted.

When more than one definition is given, each one is numbered,
and the citation illustrating it bears the corresponding number. The
place where and the exact date when a term was used are given, when-
ever possible. Sometimes a native of one Italian city is writing in an-
other part of Italy or in a foreign land. When this fact can be deter-
mined, it is stated. This information is of value because it explains
the introduction of Venetian words into the vocabulary of a Florentine

INTRODUCTION xix

or of French words into that of an Italian doing business in France.
The dates have been given as found in the sources, whether they were
new or old style, except in a very instances when (0.S.) is used after a
date—the difference of a few months would ordinarily be of no signifi-
cance for the purpose of the Glossary.

Capitals are used for the first word at the beginning of each quota-
tion even though the citation begins in the middle of a sentence. Omis-
sions of words, etc., are shown by the customary four dots.

The appendices in many instances contain explanations or citations
that are too long for the body of the Glossary. References to such
explanatory and illustrative material in the appendices are given under
numerous terms. In the appendices letters supplied in the extension
of abbreviated words have been italicized.

WoRD-DIVISION, SPELLING, ETC., IN THE CITATIONS

Word-division, punctuation, accentuation, and capitalization have
been modernized, both in quotations from printed sources and from
manuscripts. The adoption of modern word-division results in some
strange-looking forms, e.g., a fiorini, a ffare, che Mi, e altro. Apos-
trophes have been inserted wherever missing.

On the whole, the spelling has been retained—unless we regard
the separation of words, and the adding of apostrophes and accent-
marks as, essentially, changes in spelling. A few exceptions must be
noted: (1) x and v have been interchanged according to modern usage,
e.g., vino has been written as vino; vole, vuole; chiouo, chiovo; (2) ¢ has
been transcribed as 2, e.g., cavego, cavez(z)o; (3) & has been transcribed
as e although ef would probably be closer to the original meaning of the
symbol; (4) long i (j) has been changed to i, e.g., dj panj finj, di pani
fini. On the other hand, the long z has been retained or even inserted
where it was not used as the final letter in Roman numerals, e.g., x7j.

There are discrepancies and inconsistencies in word-division and
abbreviations of money signs due to the copying of so many published
sources with differing methods. I have tried whenever possible to make
the money abbreviations uniform, using f. in place of fior. as the symbol
for florins, J. for lire, s. for soldi, and d. for denari. D. and duc. will
both be found for ducat. Lib., 1b., and lbr. are used for libre, meaning
money, and for libbre, meaning pound weight.

The abbreviations for “and Company” (e compagni or e compagnia)
found in the Medici documents have been rendered as C** unless
compagni was clearly meant.

Whenever later readings of a manuscript in print have corrected
errors in earlier readings, the corrected readings have been adopted.

XX INTRODUCTION

Professor Armando Sapori, in an article and in his book, Una Compag-
nia di Calimala, corrects errors in Emiliani-Giudici’s edition of the
Statute of the Arte di Calimala of 1332 in Florence. His corrections
have cleared up the meaning of several terms which had long been
misinterpreted, such as affettatori and affetto, which should read assetta-
tori and assetto. Dr Allan Evans has carefully collated the printed
text of Pegolotti's Pratica della Mercatura with the only extant
manuscript. I have followed the corrected text which is found in Dr
Evans’ still unpublished edition and translation of Pegolotti, now on
deposit in Widener Library, Harvard University.

It is a pleasure to acknowledge my indebtedness to numerous
scholars for advice and criticism. I owe most of all to Professor N. S.
B. Gras, the Director of the Project, whose stimulating interest and
helpful suggestions have constantly encouraged and guided me. In
addition I am particularly indebted to the members of the Advisory
Committee, to Professors Mario Casella, J. D. M. Ford, C. H. Grand-
gent, W. A. Hosmer, Alfredo Schiaffini, and A. P. Usher, to Dr Louis
F. Solano, and to Messrs G. W. Cottrell, P. H. Harris, and others for
generous advice and valuable assistance. I am extremely grateful to
Dr Allan Evans for reading and criticising the entire manuscript of the
Glossary and for the use of his translation of Pegolotti’s Pratica della
Mercatura.

FLORENCE EDLER

CAMBRIDGE, MASSACHUSETTS

Bonolis, Guido. 1 diritto marittimo medievale dell’ Adriatico (Pisa, 1921).

— “Sull’industria della lana in Firenze,” Archivio storico italiano, Series V, Vol.
XXXII (1903), pp. 379-417. An article inspired by Doren’s work, emphasizing
the growth of capitalism and industrialism, with the resulting loss of independ-
ence for most of the wool-workers. Comparisons are made with similar con-
ditions in Pisa and elsewhere.

Byrne, Eugene H. “Commercial contracts of the Genoese in the Syrian Trade of
the Twelfth Century,” Quarterly Journal of Economics, XXXI (1916), 127-70.

Davidsohn, Robert. ‘Garbowolle und Garbotuche,” Historische Vierteljahrschrift,
N. F., Vol. VII (1904), pp. 385-90. Discussion of the original meaning of
Garbo wool and Garbo cloth.

Ferrara, Francesco. ‘Gli antichi banchi di Venezia,” Nuova Antologia, XVI (1871),
177-213, 435-66. History of Venetian private banks of the 14th to 16th
century.

Gras, N. S. B. “Bills of Exchange,” Encyclopaedia of the Social Sciences, II, 539 f.

Huvelin, Paul. Essai historique sur le droit des marchés et des foires. Paris, 1897.

— ‘“Quelques données nouvelles sur les foires de Champagne: I. Les courriers
des foires,” Annales de droit commercial et industrielle, XII (1898), 376-92.

Lattes, Alessandro. Il diritto commerciale nelle legislazione statutaria delle città
italiane. Milan, 1884. A comparative study of mediaeval Italian commercial
law.

— “Francesco di Marco da Prato,” Rivista del diritto commerciale, XXVII (1929),
99-103. Excellent review of Bensa’s book on Francesco Datini.

— “Genova nella storia del diritto cambiario italiano,” Riv. dir. comm., XIII!
(1915), 185-99,

— ‘Note per la storia del diritto commerciale,” Riv. dir. comm., III (1905),
474-82; V (1907), 268-81; VI (1908), 351-69; IX! (1911), 27-53; XVII (1919),
616-20; XXV! (1927), 142-44; XXVIII! (1930), 744-47; XXX! (1932), 584-87.
Very valuable notes on the history of many mediaeval commercial practices,
etc., upon which I have drawn heavily for explanations of numerous terms.

Leyerer,C. ‘Historische Entwicklung der Buchfiihrung seit der ersten Kenntnis bis
zum XVIII Jahrhundert,” Zeitschrift fiir Handelswissenschaftliche Forschung,
XV (1922), 123-52. A brief survey of the history of bookkeeping from ancient
times until the 17th century, with most emphasis on the 15th and 16th centuries.
Numerous illustrations taken from the Italian account books of Ragusa (1422-
31).

Marius, John. Advice concerning Bills of Exchange (3rd ed. London, 1674). A 17th-
century English treatise on bills of exchange.

Murray, David. Chapters in the History of Bookkeeping, Accountancy and Com-
mercial Arithmetic (Glasgow, 1930).

History of the bill of exchange.

— “Der Kurierdienst zwischen Italien und den Messen von Champagne,” Archiv
fiir Post und Telegraphie, XXIV (1896), 542-50, 571-81. A study of the courier

— “Studien zur Geschichte und Natur des dltesten Cambium,” Jahrbiicher fiir

— “The Origin of the Bill of Exchange,” Journal of Political Economy, XXII

Accomanda; 1. the Latin commenda contract of partnership (dating
back to the 10th cent. or earlier) according to which the investing
partner furnished goods or money to the traveling partner, to be

sold or invested by the latter as directed, or as he thought best.

The investor usually received 3, and the other partner, + of the

profits. See Byrne, Quar. Jour. of Econ., XX XI, 127-170; Silber-
schmidt, Die Commenda in threr friihesten Entwicklung. For another
example, see accomandatario; cf. accomandigia (2), accomandita
comanda. 2. a deposit of money or other valuables for safe-keeping
(either in a monastery or with a firm); cf. accomandigia (1).

Accomandigia; 1. a deposit or loan of goods or money (made to a
merchant or banker, prob. with the understanding that the funds
could be used for trade, the depositor being entitled to some form

1 In the Middle Ages it was customary for some monasteries to accept deposits of money and
goods for safe-keeping. A receipt, in the form of a tally of wood or parchment, was given to the
depositor. Probably in most monasteries deposits could be withdrawn only by the original depositor,
but the monks of St. Jacques, of Provins, returned deposits to anyone who presented the keys and
the tally. The Sienese merchants in Champagne, who could not make deposits in person or in their
own names, because Siena was under the interdict after the battle of Montaperti (1260), had their
merchant friends from Parma deposit valuables for them in the monastery of St. Jacques, of Pro-
vins, but they (the Sienese) could withdraw their deposits by merely presenting the keys and tallies.

Assicuratore; underwriter of marine insurance.

Al nome di Dio—a ddì x di luglio 1397. Sia manifesto a chi leggerà o udirà leggere
questa scritta fatta dell’anno e mese detti disopra che Francesco di Marco e Domenico di
Cambio e compagnia presono sicurtà per scudi [2100] d’oro sopra balle sei e uno fardello di
merci sottile cariche o si deono caricare a Mutrone per le mani di Lionardo d’Andrea
Ciampelli o d’altri per loro, in sulla nave boccia padroneggiata per Perino Conciati, o per
altro padrone che la padroneggiasse, e della detta roba carica e si dee caricare in sulla detta
nave in nome e segno di Domenico Ambruogi, segnata così [mark] ed è di valuta di scudi
[blank] o circa; e pigliano la sicurtà da Mutrone per insino in Aqua morta, posta e scarica
in terra a salvamento. Gli assicuratori sono [blank] di rischio e sicurtà [blank] la detta
roba è carica o si dee caricare a Mutrone sulla detta nave per le mani di Lionardo d'Andrea
Ciampelli o d’altro per loro.

E il rischio che gli assicuratori corrono in sulla detta roba, carica, o si dee caricare in
sulla detta nave, si è dall’ora che la detta nave farà vela o avesse fatto vela da Mutrone per
andare in Aqua morta; si è di Dio, di mare, di gente, di fuoco, di gitto di mare; di riteni-
mento di signori o di Comuni, o d’alcun’altra persona, o di rappresaglia o d’arresto e
d’ogni altro caso, pericolo, fortuna, impedimento o caso sinistro, che per verun modo ne
potesse intervenire o fusse intervenuto, e fussono fatti i casi come si volessero o di che
condizione, salvo di stiva o di dogana, tutti gli portano a tutti gli corrono i detti assicura-
tori sopra di loro per insino a tanto che la detta roba sarà posta e scarica in terra a sal-
vamento in Aqua morta.

E se per caso avvenisse che la detta roba carica in sulla detta nave, e partita, o partirà, di
detto luogo per andare a detto luogo, ne intervenisse o fosse intervenuto alcuno disastro,
del quale Iddio guardi, giunte le vere novelle del disastro, dal dì a mesi due prossimi
che seguiranno, i detti assicuratori si promettono e obbligansi di dare e di pagare a
detti Francesco di Marco e Domenico di Cambio e compagnia caduno quella quantità
di denari per lui assicurati.

E se per caso avvenisse che la detta roba carica in sulla detta nave e partita, o partirà, da
detto luogo per andare a detto luogo, infra mesi sei prossimi che seguiranno non ce ne
avesse vere novelle, che in quello caso i detti assicuratori si promettono e obbligansi di
dare e pagare a detto Francesco di Marco e Domenico di Cambio e compagnia caduno
quello quantità di denari per lui assicurati.

E se per caso avvenisse che passati i mesi sei di che di sopra si contiene, e la roba giug-
nesse dappoi e scaricassesi in terra a salvamento in Aqua morta, che in questo caso i detti
Francesco di Marco e Domenico di Cambio e compagnia siano tenuti e debbano rendere
e restituire a caduno dei detti assicuratori quella quantità di denari che per detta si-
curtà avessero ricevuti; e per le sopra dette cose osservare e attenere i detti assicuratori
sì si obbligano loro e loro rede e beni, che sono e per innanzi saranno, e sottomettonsi ad
ogni Corte, Arte e luogo della città di Firenze e specialmente alla Corte e Ufficiale e Sei
della Mercatanzia della detta città e in ogni altro luogo dovunque a’ detti Francesco di
Marco e Domenico di Cambio e compagnia gli volessono convenire e far convenire per
alcuno modo.

Bisenzone, fiere di; the so-called ‘‘Fairs of Besancon”’ (were established

after the four in Lyons, were exclusively bill fairs for the settling,
paying and issuing of bills of exchange. After a few years, the fairs
were moved to Italy, where they were held in different northern cities,
esp. in Piacenza, but the name, ‘‘Fairs of Besangon”, was retained).

una parte sono arbitrii, rivolture e girandole, e non vivi debiti o crediti effetivi. Flor-
ence, 1581: Davanzati, Notizia de’ Cambi, p. 432.

GLOSSARY OF BUSINESS TERMS 55

controlled the three groups of master artisans—assettatori, cloth

Calimala merchants. The industry of finishing imported cloth was

century due to difficulty in obtaining cloth in France and Flanders
and to the development of the manufacture of cloth in Florence and

Comandamento; the lower and briefer part of a notarial contract for a

GLOSSARY OF BUSINESS TERMS 79

essential elements of the obligation in a concise form, plus the formula
of guarantee used by notaries where the law authorized them to
give executive force to the acts they drew up. The lender sometimes
retained both carta and comandamento, sometimes, only one or the
other).

Corriere di pagamento; courier of payment one of two couriers sent

thirtieth day of each fair. The second probably arrived at the
beginning of the period of payment with paper, i.e., bills of exchange,
etc., and left at the end of this period to notify merchants in Florence
of their financial obligations).! Cf. scarselliere del pagamento.

Garbo, panno di; Garbo cloth (i.e., cloth made with Garbo wool, in

Garzaria*; workshop of a master workman who napped or teaseled
cloth, in which merchants sometimes displayed their cloth for sale
(in Padua and Vicenza). In Padua, by the end of the 14th
century the name was given to a quadrangle of buildings belonging to
the Wool Gild, in which were located not only the shops of master
workmen who teaseled cloth, but also those of masters who sorted,
carded, and spun wool, the offices of the Gild, a washing establish-
ment for cloth, and a cloth warehouse. See Rizzoli, Arte Lana in
Padova, pp. 26 f.

Seta paga uno diritto che s’appella giusso, che è 10 per cento. E sì tosto come lo legno in

lo detto diritto della seta, e però si vuol essere avvisato chi l’ha in porto che avanti che
lo legno surga l’ancora in mare di patteggiare co’ doanieri. Ed elli costumano tutto
giorno di far patto a meno di 10 per cento secondo che l’uomo si puote convenire con loro;
ma dove l’uomo non trattasse patto con loro e non si accordasse con loro, ti possono
domandare e prendere interamente tutto lo detto diritto della seta, cioè 10 per cento. E
questo cotale diritto della seta è per questa medesima maniera e per tutto lo Regno.
Florence, 1340: Pegolotti, Merca., p. 187.

Lanino; originally (in Florence) an independent intermediary who
bought carded wool (lara) and had it spun by women spinners, then
sold the yarn to the industrial entrepreneurs who gave it to their
weavers to be used as weft threads. By the 15th century the lanini
had lost their independence and during the 16th century they were
agents or employees of the industrial entrepreneurs from whom they
received carded wool, which they weighed and gave out to women
spinners in the country and for which they were paid so much per
pound of yarn according to a tariff fixed by law (like the stamaiuolt),
plus an extra commission (provvisione) fixed by custom. The amount
that the spinners were to receive from the lanini was also established
by law; for example, an ordinance of 1547, renewed in 1556 and 1557,
provided that for each pound of yarn to be used for rash (lana da
rascie) the entrepreneur (Janaiuolo) must pay his lanino s.14 piccioli,
out of which sum, the Janino had to pay s.12 per pound to the
spinner, in money, never in kind, leaving a profit of 2 soldi per pound
to the Janino, plus the customary commission. According to the
Medici account books of the 16th century, each firm of lanaiuoli
employed only one lanino, in contrast to several stamaiuoli. A
careful record of the names of the spinners of carded wool and the
amounts of wool given them to be spun was kept in the firm’s books.
The wages due the spinners are not listed, only the sums due the
lanino. For other examples, see filatoio, stame. Cf. stamaiuolo.
For further information, see Appendix VIII and Doren, Wollen-
tuchindus., p. 255.

Lettera di cambio; a bill of exchange (i.e., a draft of one party upon
another, by which the first party, the drawer, requests the second
party the drawee or payer, residing in another place to pay to a
designated person, or to his order, on a fixed date or on demand, a
specified sum of money, the value of which the drawer has received
from the remitter or creditor). This term was first used in the
modern sense in the early 14th century, although the liability
of the drawer or the acceptor was not definitely established until the
end of that century. This term was replaced in the 16th century by
the modern one, tratta. For other examples, see maturare, sotto-
scribente. Cf. cambio (2), cambio per lettera (di pagamento), lettera
di pagamento, prima, seconda, terza, quarta, fare scrivere, mandare a

Lettera di pagamento; letter of payment (i.e., an early form of the bill
exchange, term used in the 13th and 14th centuries). At first it wasa
draft of one member of a firm on another or of an agent on a principal.
By the 14th century such drafts were drawn by one company upon
another, and during that century the term was used synonymously
with the newer term, lettera di cambio. The lettera di pagamento
was given or sent to the payee to be presented to the drawee for
acceptance and payment. If the bill was not honored the payee had
no redress, until the late 14th century, when the liability of the
maker in case of protest was established (Baldus, 1381). See
Huvelin, Essai, pp. 553 ff.; Lattes, Riv. dir. comm., TX, 46; XIII,
188; XXVII!, 101f.; XXX!, 584-87; Postan, Vierteljahrschrift,
XXIII, 26-75. For other examples, see lettera di contenta, terza

lettera, vantaggio (1). Cf. cambio per lettera, lettera di cambio, tratta

(2).

venni, e con questa vi mandiamo la lettera del pagamento che ’l detto Paganello

Licci; heddles (suspended threads of the loom-harness, through which
warp threads were drawn before being drawn through the teeth of the

GLOSSARY OF BUSINESS TERMS 163

reed; made of twisted, spun Provencal wool with iron eyelets
called maglie. A loom should have at least two sets of heddles,
i.e., two shaft-heddles, to form the shed through which the shuttle
passes. Florentine looms had from two to four shaft-heddles).
Cf. a tre licci, alla piana.

Le maglie vedi ai pettini mettonsi nel filo del copertoio che non lo spela, et di sotto e di
sopra alle maglia sono i licci del pettini che ssi tirano con le casse; sono della più lungha
lana provenzala si trovi filati, ighuali e come vivagni torte. E filano detta lana di licci a
roccha cioè quel calamo lungho, e unghuno con grasso di porco e bituro, e non con olio,
perchè l’olio riarderebbe . ... E basta un pettine con detti licci circha a 20 anni, ma
sempre s’aopera spesso che un mese non sta voto per volta. Et che se i stessi sei mesi che
non si aoperassi, intingnerebbe il liccio e guasterebbesi o la magla del ferro aruginerebbe
e guasterebbe il filo .... El filo dell’accia per licci roderebbe la lana . . . . Et che al
tessere de’ panni lini fanno sanza maglie pure co rischontro de’ licci, e tolgono licci
d’accia. [For weaving linen cloth, flaxen heddles were sometimes used—without iron
eyelets, but such heddles would gnaw through woolen thread.] Florence, 15th cent.:
“Tratt. lana,” Doren, Wollentuchindus., p. 493.

Licci, a tre; (loom) with three shaft-heddles or harness. (In this

expression, liccio means the group of heddles on one shaft of the
loom-harness. The Florentine loom had two, three, or four shaft-
heddles, two for plain weave, three or four for twill weave. Cloth
was sometimes named from the number of harness-frames used in
weaving it: panno a tre licci, a quatiro licci, or alla piana). See
Doren, Wollentuchindus., pp. 95 f. For example, see orditore. Cf.
licci, alla piana.

chi toglie possessioni a fitto, e le affitta altrui; perchè esse non sono merci .... Quegli

Pettine; loom-reed, a comblike wooden frame with reed or wire teeth
through which the warp threads were drawn singly or doubly, after
they had been drawn through the heddles of the loom-harness.
(Upon the width of the reed and the closeness of the teeth depended
the breadth and the fineness of weave of a cloth.) For examples,
see orditore, subbio (1).

Pettine, quarto di; a quarter of a loom-reed, i.e., a quarter of one
hundred teeth, or twenty-five teeth, a unit used in determining the
width of a reed and the cloth woven with it (in Fabriano, Padua).
(A reed of 123 quarters had 312 teeth through which warp threads
were drawn in pairs, so that such a reed called for a warp of 624
threads.) See Zonghi, Doc. Fabrianesi, p. 175.

Si ordina a tutti li tessitori che vorranno tessere nella Terra di Fabriano che possino
tessere dette rascie bianche di cento in pettini di altezza de quarti dodici e mezzo in
tredici e mezzo, e trovandosi tessere in pettini più alti caschino in pena . . . . Fabriano,
1596: Stat. artis lanae, p. 98.

there were two main divisions of the gild: membri per la maggiore—

the major division.)

1 “The brokers tell me that between friends [in Venice] exchange on Lucca is $%, not with-
standing that when they want one [a bill of exchange], there are no takers but there are a number of
drawers.” Trade between Lucca and Venice was uneven in the late fourteenth century. Lucca
imported raw silk from Venice, but she sold very little silk cloth to Venice because Lucchese silk-
merchants and artisans had introduced Lucchese methods into the Venetian silk industry in the
middle of that century. Because Lucca owed Venice much more money than Venice owed her,
drawers of drafts on Lucca were plentiful in Venice, but takers of Lucchese drafts on Venice were
scarce.

Ritenzione; 1. a deduction (of a fixed percentage—d.2 per florin—

Stamaiuolo; originally, (in Tuscany) an independent intermediary who
bought combed wool (stame) and had it spun into worsted yarn by
women spinners, then sold the yarn to the industrial entrepreneurs
who used it for the warp of all kinds of cloth (see example a). In
Florence during the 14th century, the stamazuoli lost their industrial

and financial independence and by the 16th century they had become
virtually agents or overseers of the industrial entrepreneurs, from
whom they received combed wool which they gave out to women
spinners in the country and for which they were paid so much per
pound of yarn, according to a tariff fixed by law. The amount that
the spinners were to receive from the stamaiuoli was also established
by law—for example, an ordinance of 1547, renewed in 1556 and 1557,
provided that for each pound of yarn to be used for rash (stame da
rascie) the entrepreneur (/anaiuolo) must pay his stamaiuolo 1.1 s.10
out of which sum the stamaiuolo had to pay 1.1 s.5 per pound to the
spinner in money, never in kind, leaving a commission of five soldi
per pound for the stamaiuolo. In 16th-century Florence the stama-
tuoli were annually approved by magistrates of the Grand Duke.
They must know how to read and write and were required to keep
strict account of each bundle of wool they received to be spun,
checking the weight before and after spinning, on their own scales
which had 12} ounces to the pound, listing the name of each spinner
to whom wool was given with the wage the spinner was to receive.
They were forbidden to take wool from each other. They were
evidently free to choose their own spinners, and, according to the

280 GLOSSARY OF BUSINESS TERMS

Medici account books of the 16th century, the entrepreneur did not
keep a record of the names of the spinners employed by his stamaiu-
oli (who were required to keep their own records), as he did for the
spinners employed by his Janino, or agent who handled the carded
wool for spinning. The Medici, in the year 1555 employed four
stamaiuoli and only one lanino. The stamaiuoli were frequently
slow in returning yarn, sometimes taking five or six months to return
the last of a given lot of stame. For further information, see Ap-
pendix VIII and Doren, Wollentuchindus., pp. 150 f., 245, 247, 248,
256. For other examples, see lanino, stame.

non potere risquotere li stami l’un dell’altro dalle filatrici predette sotto dette pene. Et

Tacca; a label or tag (of either wood or parchment fastened to cloth
imported by Florentine merchants from France and Flanders, which
contained the sum of most of the cost items of the cloth, i.e., the
original sale price, God’s penny, wrapping, warehouse taxes, dues and
tolls of the town where the cloth was purchased and the maltéte of
the French king, porters’ fees and tips, and any dyeing and finishing
of the cloth done in the place of its provenience after the purchase.
Carriage, except between Caen and Paris, and discount on exchange
were not included. When the cloth was dyed or refinished in
Florence, the expenses involved were added, as a second sum, to
the tag). Cf. scritta (5), segno (5), taccamento, taccare.

dyers with woad were in a class apart from the other dyers. In

Torsello; a long flat bale (something like the torso of a statue in shape,
covered with felt, canvas, etc.; usually transported by a pack-animal;
used esp. for shipping all kinds of cloth. The torsello was the emblem
of several cloth gilds, e.g., the Calimala, in Florence, and the Silk
merchants of Lucca. The number of pieces of cloth which a balla
or torsello might contain was sometimes regulated by statute. Small
bundles were frequently shipped inside the bales). For other
examples, see dalla (a), fardello (a). Cf. balla, fagotto, fascio, ghilla.

Trama; 1. weft-yarn for woolen cloth, i.e., the kind of yarn usually

1 “And also we inform you [Jacomo Cacciaconti in France, a member of a Sienese partnership]
that we have sold 106 livres prov. to Jachamo Ubertini, a money-changer, to be paid at the Fair of
St. John, 1260, and we sold them at the rate of 33 soldi the dozen [livres prov.], and we have been paid.
Therefore you will pay [the money] to Rinbotto Buonaiuti for him [Ubertini] at his pleasure.” An
example of a letter of advice (lettera di avviso) sent directly from the drawer of a bill of exchange to
the drawee, ordering him to pay a certain sum to a third party. At the same time, and usually by
the same courier, the remitter sent a notice to receive the money to the payee. The letter of pay-
ment (bill of exchange) might be separate or embodied in a letter addressed to the payee. The
above example of a letter of advice was embodied in a long letter sent by the partners in Siena to
their member in Champagne. During the thirteenth century such letters of advice took the place
of the earlier notarial instruments of exchange when merchants or bankers had associates abroad in
the place in which a draft was domiciled. In the fourteenth century the letter of advice was gradu-
ally abandoned as unnecessary, leaving only the letter of payment or draft. See Schaube, Zeit.
gesamm. Handelsrecht, XLIII, 9-23; Lattes, Riv. dir. comm., 1X", 46; Sayous, Rev. hist. du droit fran. et
etran. (Jan.—Mars, 1933), 101 f.

CLASSIFIED LISTS
1, FLORENTINE MONEY USED IN THE MEDICI ACCOUNTS

Kinps oF FLORINS:

Fiorino d’oro: gold florin (3.53) coined from 1252 until the first half of the
fifteenth century.

Fiorino di suggello: sealed florin, originally the same as the above, but tested
for weight and sealed in a box or purse. About 1450 it became a money of
account for silver.

Fiorino largo: large gold florin which first appeared about 1450. 20% better
than the fiorino di suggello.

Fiorino largo di grossi: a large florin of groats, a money of account for silver.

Fiorino largo d’oro in oro: large gold florin in gold, used from ca. 1482 to 1530.
19% better than the fiorino largo di grossi.

Money or Account:!

1 petty lira (lira di piccioli)—20 petty soldi—240 petty denari.

1 lira a fiorino—20 soldi a fiorino—240 denari a fiorino.

any gold florin above—29 soldi a fiorino—348 denari a fiorino.

any gold florin—20 soldi a oro—240 denari a oro.

BASE Coins:
1 Quattrino—4 denari.
1 Grosso—y'; of a gold florin (variable).

2. LINEAR MEASURES

Accono and Ancona: arm’s length (in Altoluogo, Turkey).

Alla: ell (in England, France, and Flanders).

Braccio: arm’s length (in Italy). 3-4 braccta = 1 canna; ca. 22-26 inches.

Canna: cane, cloth measure, ell (in Italy, S. France, Majorca, etc.); 3-4 braccia =
1 canna; ca. 24-3 yards.

Corda: ca. 5 Florentine canne (in Provence).

Covido: ca. 1 Florentine braccio (in Lisbon).

Godo: gode, used for measuring cottons, flannels, etc. (in England); more than one
English ell, ca. 2 braccia.

Ona: aune, ell (the same as alla).

Palmo: palm, hand’s breadth (in Naples, Sicily, Rome); ‘ca. 4-4 of a Florentine
canna.

Passino: length of a warp-frame, 7 Florentine braccia, used as a measure for the warp
and for cloth.

1 The terms in italics are money of account.

318 CLASSIFIED LISTS

Picco: pic or pike, (in Egypt, Turkey, and the Levant); ca. one braccio.
Picco di Gazeria: Gazeria pic, used for measuring linens (in Constantinople).
Quarro: % of a braccio (in Lucca, Siena).

Quarta and Quarto: 1 of a braccio (in Florence, Venice).

Varra: vara, cloth measure (in Seville); ca. 24 Florentine Braccia.

Verga: verge, yard (in England).

3. DRY MEASURES

Alghiero: ca. 1 Florentine bushel (in Lisbon).

Anco: 7'z of a cafisso (in Seville).

Barrata: a grain measure (in Provence).

Barzella: + of a cafisso (in Valencia).

Bustello: English bushel, 7g of a quarter.

Cafisso: dry measure (in N. Africa and Spain); varies from 7 to 26 bushels.

Cantare and Cantaro: 5 Venetian bushels (in Tana).

Carica: 6-7 Venetian bushels (in Beirut).

Carro: ca. 22 Venetian bushels (in Apulia).

Cascito and Chisteto: 5-84 Venetian bushels (in Tana).

Corba: ca. Florentine bushels (in Perugia).

Mina: ca.13-4 Florentine bushels (in Genoa and S. France).

Moggio: ca. 4-52 Florentine bushels (in Italy, S. France, Turkey, the Levant); 24

17. STEPS IN THE MANUFACTURE OF WOOLEN CLOTH IN ITALY

The order of the steps is based on a Florentine treatise of the fifteenth century,
“Trattato dell’ Arte della Lana,” published in Alfred Doren, Die Florentiner W ollentuch-

(1) Willeying: a preliminary cleaning of fleeces from dust, etc., by beating with

battitore di boldroni: willyer, workman who beat fleeces.
MANUFACTURE OF WOOLEN CLOTH 325

(2) Sorting of fleeces and different parts of fleeces according to quality of wool.
cernere and sortire: to sort (wool).
sceglitore: wool-sorter, who tore different parts of fleece from each other and
separated them into piles, according to quality.
sceglitoio: wool-sorting table.
pugnea and ravvolto: fleece rolled into a ball or bundle.

(3) Washing and scouring of wool and drying on tables.
lavatore: wool-washer.

(4) Cleansing wool of impurities by hand and with small scissors.
spelazzare: to pick over wool (after washing) to remove foreign matter.
vagliare: to shake wool in a sieve (after washing) to remove foreign matter.
divettare: to pick over wool (cutting out knots and bits of skin).
divettino: wool-cleanser.
divettatura: the cleansing of wool (from knots, etc.).
(The wool was dyed at this point, if it was to be dyed in the wool at all.)

(5) Beating and spraying wool with water.
battitore: place where wool was beaten.
battere ad arco, scamare, scamatare, sgammaitare, and vergheggiare: to
beat (wool).
battilano, scamatino, vergheggiatore, and vergheggino: wool-beater.
scamatatura: beating (of wool).
arco: wool-beater’s implement.
camato and sgammaito: wool-beater’s rod.
faldella: a quantity of wool (ca. 7-10 lbs.) after it had been beaten.
pennello di peneri: bristle brush for moistening wool during beating.

(6) Greasing or oiling of wool. (Usually done by wool-comber.)
ungere: to grease (wool).
bagnare con olio: to oil (wool).

(7) Combing of wool (both long and short staple).
pettinare: to comb (wool).
pettinatore: wool-comber.
pettinatrice: wool-comber (fem.).
pettinatura: combed wool.

(8) Placing combed wool on distaffs for spinning.

appennecchiare: to arrange (combed wool) on a distaff.

appenecchino: workman who arranged wool upon distaffs.

pennecchio: bunch of wool arranged on distaff.

appennecchiatura: arranging of wool on distaff.

calamo: long, combed wool (which was spun from distaff and used for warp).
stame: combed wool (for a warp).

326

CLASSIFIED LISTS

(9) Preparing short wool (left over from combing process) for carding by picking it

over, spraying and oiling it.
palmella: wool-combings.

(10) Carding (short wool).

carteggiare, scardassare, scartezare, and scartigliare: to card (wool).

scardassatore, scardassiere, scardazzature, scarteggino, and scartezatore:
wool-carder.

cardo, scardasso, and scartacio: carding-comb.

lana: carded wool (in contrast to stame, combed wool).

(11) Spinning.

filare: to spin (wool).

filatore: spinner.

filatrice, filatora, and filiera: spinner (fem.).

filatoio: spinning-wheel (used for carded wool; distaff, used for combed wool).
molinello: spinning-wheel.

rocca: distaff (for combed wool).

mazzo: ball (of yarn).

(12) Winding of yarn on reels.

incannare: to wind (yarn) on reels.
cannone: reel for winding yarn.

(13) Measuring off the warp.

ordire: to measure off the warp.

orditore: warper, who measured off the warp on the warp-frame.

orditrice and orditora: warper (fem.).

orditoio: warp-frame (on which the correct number of threads of the desired
length were measured off).

orditura, ordimento, and tela: warp, warp-threads.

passino: length of a warp-frame, usually 7 braccia.

paiuola: unit of forty threads wound on one peg of a warp-frame.

porta and portata: unit of forty threads.

mezzetta: one-half of a portata, or twenty threads.

subbio: warp-beam upon which warp was wound after being measured and
sized.

licci: heddles (of loom-harness through which warp was drawn).

pettine: loom-reed (through the teeth of which warp was drawn after the
heddles).

quarto di pettine: a quarter of a loom-reed or 25 teeth (unit of measure in
determining length of reed).

lenzatura and lenzo: warp of selvage.

MANUFACTURE OF WOOLEN CLOTH Sdf

(13a) Sizing the warp threads with dressing paste (done by the warper, or by the

weaver before winding threads on warp-beam).
imbozzimare: to size the warp with dressing paste.
bozzima: weaver’s or dressing paste for sizing the warp-threads.

(13b) Beaming and drawing warp-threads through heddles and reed (done by the

weaver, or his assistants).

(14) Weaving of cloth

tessere and texare: to weave (cloth).

tessitore, testore, texitore, and tessaro: weaver.

tessitora and tessitrice: weaver (fem.).

telaio and telaro: loom.

teleria: looms, also place where looms were used, i.e., weavers’ homes.

calcola: treadle (of a loom).

carrucola: pulley, connected with treadle to work shaft-heddles up and down.

subbio: warp-beam, cloth-roll.

spuola: weaver’s shuttle.

cannello: bobbin for weaver’s shuttle.

licci, a tre: (loom) with three shaft-heddles.

piana, alla: (loom) with four shaft-heddles.

trama: weft, woof.

lana: weft yarn (in contrast to stame or tela).

penero and pedano: free ends of warp left over after weaving.

cordone: unit of ten warp threads into which free ends were divided and
probably plaited.

posta: some kind of mark placed at head of piece of cloth to designate its
breadth and quality.

cordellina: a twisted selvage.

panella, vivagno, cimossa, and orice: selvage.

Finishing of Woven Cloth

(15) Burling, i.e., removing knots, rough places, etc., from cloth.

dizzeccolare, dizoccolare, and rivedere: to burl (cloth).
dizzeccolatore and riveditore: burler.

zeccolo: knot in woolen cloth.

riveditura: burling (of cloth).

(16) Scouring and washing of cloth.

purgare: to scour or wash (cloth).

terrare: to scour cloth with fuller’s earth to remove grease and dressing-paste.
curatore: scourer (of cloth).

pulcatore and purgatore: scourer, washer.

pulco and purgo: scouring of cloth, or place where cloth was scoured.

piscina: large tub for washing wool, cloth, etc.

purgatura: scouring (of cloth).

CLASSIFIED LISTS

(16a) Sometimes a second burling after washing, or after the first napping on the

wrong side of cloth.

(17) Fulling of cloth.

conciare, follare, gualcare, saldare, sodare, and valcare: to full (cloth by
soaping and treading on it in fullers’ vat or by using a fulling mill).

spremere: to wring (water out of fulled cloth).

calcatore, follatore, folaore, gualcatore, gualcherano, gualchieraio, valcarano,
and valcatore: fuller.

folla, gualcatura, and valcatura: fulling process.

folo, gualchiera, gualco, valca, and valchera: fulling-mill.

cavallitta: apparatus for hoisting cloth (used by fullers).

pila: stone or brick basin for washing and fulling cloth.

pilata: amount of cloth that a pila could hold.

(18) Tentering or stretching and drying of cloth.

tirare, stirare, and distirare: to stretch (cloth).

tiratore, tiratoiaio, chiodaruolo, and cloarolo: tenderer, who stretched cloth
after it came from fulling-mill.

tiratoio and tiratoro: apparatus for stretching cloth, or place where cloth
was stretched.

chioara, chiovara, and cloara: stretching and drying frame for cloth.
tiratura: stretching of cloth.

(19) Teaseling or napping, done with teasels (thistle-heads) or teaseling cards to

raiseanaponcloth. (The first teaseling was done on damp cloth.)
cardare, conciare da cardo, and raccardare: to teasel or nap (cloth).
cardata: napping.
cardatura and garzatura: shavings from teaseling (of cloth).
cardatore, conciatore da cardo, garzatore, and garzaore: teaseler, napper.

garzaria: central workshop where cloth was teaseled and sheared.
carto and cardo: fuller’s teasel.

pelo: nap (of cloth).

riversare and roversare: to prepare nap for shearing (after teaseling by raising
it with a riversetia).

(20) Shearing of cloth. (First shearing done on damp cloth.)

accimare, avvistare, cimare, zimmare, and tondere: to shear (cloth).
cimatore, and tonditore: shearman or cropper.
cimatura: shearing process.

tondatura: shavings from the shearing of cloth.

(21) Dyeing of cloth (if dyed wool or yarn was not used in weaving).

tingere, tignere, tingnere, tegnare, and tenzere: to dye (wool, cloth, etc.).
tintore, tignetore, tingitore, tegnitore, tentore, vagellaio, and vagellaro:
dyer.

CLASSES OF WOOL-WORKERS 329

tintore di guado: dyer who used woad and indigo.

tintore dell’arte maggiore: dyer who used madder.

tintura: dyeing process.

tinta: dyeing and dyehouse.

tino: dyer’s vat.

vagello: mixture of grit, alum, and water which formed basis of blue dyes.

(21a) Another stretching and drying of cloth after dyeing, as is stated in the manu-
script.

(22) Mending or drawing of cloth (to correct defects, such as holes and missing
yarn). (Sometimes done directly after burling.)
emendare: to mend, to draw (new cloth).
rimendare: to mend, to draw.
emendatore, mendatore, and rimendatore: mender or drawer.
rimendatura: mending (of new cloth).

(23) Second and subsequent napping and shearing. (Done on dry cloth.) (Cloth
was napped and sheared two to four times depending on the fineness of the

cloth.)

(24) Napping of cloth lightly after final shearing.
accottonare, cottonare, and gottonare: to comb woolen cloth slightly after
final shearing to give cloth a nap of fine hairs lying in one direction.
accottonatura: slight napping.

(25) Pressing of cloth (done with a cold press in Middle Ages).
manganare: to press (new cloth).
manganatura: pressing of new cloth.
cartone, dare il (al panno): to give a lustre to cloth by pressing between

sheets of paper.

(26) Folding of cloth (for packing).
piegare and plecare: to fold (cloth).

18. CLASSES OF WOOL-WORKERS IN FLORENCE

I. Centralized Manufacture: laborers who worked in the central workshop of an
industrial entrepreneur for day wages.
williers
sorters
beaters
oilers

carders
appennecchini, who arranged combed wool on distaff for spinning

330 CLASSIFIED LISTS

*warpers

II. Dependent Wholesale Handicraft: small masters, more or less independent, who
worked at home on material furnished by an entrepreneur for piece wages.
spinners ;
warpers (also in sec. I)
weavers

III. Large establishments (owned either privately or by gilds) in which small masters
rented space and apparatus.
wool washers
cloth washers and fullers
stretchers and dryers

IV. Independent Wholesale Handicraft: master workmen with private shops.
dyers

19. STEPS IN THE MANUFACTURE OF SILK CLOTH IN ITALY

(1) Reeling of the filaments from cocoons to form skeins. (Several cocoons were
unwound together to form a loose thread.)

trarre: to unwind cocoons and to reel the filaments into skeins.

(Silk was usually purchased by Italian merchants already reeled, i.e., the reeling
was usually done where the cocoons were raised.)

(2) Winding skeins of reeled silk on reels or bobbins.
incannare: to wind silk on a cannone, reel.
faccitrice and maestra: female silk worker who wound silk.

(3) Throwing of silk to make thread (corresponds to the spinning of wool, flax, etc.).
filare: to twist silk with left-handed turns (the first twisting given to warp
threads).
torcere: to throw or twist silk from left to right (the second twisting for warp

threads and the only one given to weft threads).
filatoiaio, filatore, filatrice, and torcitore: throwster.
faccitrice and maestra: female silk worker who threw silk.
guindalo and guindolo: reel or bobbin used by throwster.

“Some worked at home or in a private workshop.

MANUFACTURE OF SILK CLOTH 331

(4) Steaming of silk (in a dyehouse).
stufare: to steam (silk).

(5) Boiling of silk in a soap solution to remove gummy substance (about one-fourth
of the weight is lost).
cuocere: to boil (silk).
cocitore: artisan who boiled (silk).
seta cotta: boiled silk.

(6) Rewinding on reels or bobbins.
incannare: to wind silk on a reel.

(7) Warping of silk.
ordire: to warp.
orditora: warper.
orsoio: organzine, warp threads.

(8) Weaving of silk cloth.
testore, testrice, and textore: weaver.
licciaruolo: boy who pulled the strings attached to the loom which raised
or lowered the threads of the warp.
tela: warp.
ristagno: special warp threads.
| testoio and trama: weft threads.
pelo: pile.
volta: unit of 40-70 silk warp threads.

(9) Dyeing of silk.
tintore di seta: dyer of silk.

APPENDIX I
MEDICI PARTNERSHIPS

Much has been written on the subject of the temporary partnerships formed for
one venture, or one sea voyage only, in the maritime cities of Italy and other countries
during the Middle Ages. These were of two types: the commenda and the societas
maris. In Italian cities of the interior, on the other hand, the typical form of partner-
ship, both for trade and for industry, was the compagnia, a partnership of several
years’ duration, and one in which, with few exceptions, each partner made some
contribution to the capital. Originally the compagnia was a family partnership, but
by the first quarter of the thirteenth century, outsiders were occasionally taken in,
especially factors who were made junior partners.

Partnership in one form or another is characteristic of mediaeval business,
especially of commerce. The individual merchant trading on his own behalf is the
exception. Small local shopkeepers and artisans were less likely to form partnerships
than bankers, entrepreneurs in industries, and international merchants, but partner-
ships were not uncommon among certain classes of artisans, such as wool-washers,
cloth finishers, and especially dyers, in Florence. Companies formed by such
artisans are frequently referred to in the Medici account books of the fifteenth and
sixteenth centuries.

Practically all the industrial entrepreneurs in Florence and Lucca and probably
elsewhere formed partnerships for the manufacture of woolen and silk cloth. Some-
times these were for the control of processes, much like the modern vertical combina-
tion; that is to say, an entrepreneur or a company of industrial entrepreneurs formed
a partnership with dyers, finishers of cloth, etc. Such partnerships may have been
fairly common in an earlier period, but by the fifteenth century they appeared less
frequently in Florence, although there are a few examples of Medici entrepreneurs in
the woolen industry forming partnerships with dyers and with soapmakers in the
fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Partnerships with dyers are found in both cen-
turies. The two with soapmakers date from the first quarter of the sixteenth
century. But according to the data yielded by the Medici Manuscripts it was more
usual for a merchant of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries to form several partner-
ships for the manufacture of cloth and its sale in Florence and abroad. Some of the
Medici wool-merchants were also bankers or dealt in articles of luxury, such as jewels,
gold and silver ornaments, etc.

I shall illustrate the kinds of partnership and the interrelation of partnerships
among the Medici by outlining the careers of two or more Medici merchants based
upon account books, letter books, and articles of association. The Selfridge
Collection contains one volume of partnership agreements, the oldest of which is

335

336 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

from 14271 It was not customary to have a notary draw up the terms of a partner-
ship. One of the partners, or an employee, especially a bookkeeper, usually drew
up the articles, which were then signed by each partner. There is great similarity
between the different partnership agreements in the Medici volume in wording, items,
and arrangement, so that one was apparently copied from another with only the
necessary changes in dates, names of partners, capital, percentages of profit, etc.
These articles are also very similar in arrangement and terminology to those partner-
ship agreements of the fourteenth century for Florence and other Tuscan cities, some
of which have already been published.

The Medici partnerships were usually formed for a three-year period. One
example of a five-year agreement for a bank has been found.? With this exception,
all the partnerships referred to in this appendix were for three years. They were
renewable for two years, and then again for two more, and so on, until some one
expressed a desire to withdraw, or one of the partners died. The articles of associa-
tion usually provided that the renewal would take place automatically, unless a
partner notified his fellow partner or partners at least six months in advance of his
desire to withdraw at the end of the three-year term. In the fifteenth-century con-
tracts, nothing is stated concerning the form or manner in which a notice of with-
drawal was to be given. Presumably an oral notice would suffice.?

In the earliest partnership agreement of the sixteenth century (1506) and in all
the succeeding ones of that century, a phrase, introduced into the withdrawal clause,
showed the manner in which notice of withdrawal was to be given. There were two
ways: (1) the partner might record his notice of approaching withdrawal in writing in
the section of the journal called “Records” or “Memoranda” (Ricordanze), or in a
separate book, if the Ricordanze were kept apart from the journal; (2) he might notify
the Wool Gild (if the partnership was one for the cloth trade or industry or for the
dyeing of cloth) of his intention to withdraw.‘

The first Medici merchant to be studied is one who was interested only in the
manufacture and sale of woolen cloth, and chiefly as a silent partner rather than an
active one. His name is Bernardo d’Antonio de’ Medici and he died in 1465. The
earliest record of his business activities is found in a ledger, M.S 496, for a partnership
in the manufacture of fine woolen cloth from English wool, formed in 1431 by
Bernardo’s brother, Giovenco d’Antonio, and his cousin, Giovenco di Giuliano.
Giovenco d’Antonio contributed 1000 florins and was to receive two-thirds of the
profits. His cousin contributed only 300 florins and was to receive one-third of the

2 MS 560 (4) fol. 152°.
