profits. Both partners were to be active in the business. Bernardo did not enter
the partnership, but he deposited 1000 florins with the company, on which amount
he was to receive 10% interest? The partnership was for three years. This was
the customary term for Medici partnerships. At the end of that period, the books
showed a profit of 700 florins. When the partnership expired, Bernardo entered into
a partnership with his brother and his cousin as the dominant partner, investing 2200
florins himself, The name of the new firm was to be “Bernardo d’Antonio de’
Medici and Company.” His brother invested 1500 florins, or approximately his
capital plus his profit from the old partnership. Giovenco di Giuliano again con-
tributed only 300 florins. In the first partnership both cousins had been active
partners. In the new one only Giovenco di Giuliano had to give full time to the
business and could not enter into any other mercantile association. Bernardo and
his brother, Giovenco d’Antonio, were free to give as much or as little time to the
partnership as they saw fit, and to participate in other business activities. The
active partner, Giovenco di Giuliano, was to receive no salary, but was to draw his
share of the profits on the basis of 900 florins instead of the 300 florins he invested
as capital. Giovenco d’Antonio was to draw for 1300 florins instead of 1500, and
Bernardo for 1800, in place of the 2200 florins he contributed to the capital.*

Giovenco d’Antonio had kept the books for the old partnership, but as he was
no longer to be an active partner, a bookkeeper, Giovanni di Bencini, was engaged.*
No account book is extant for this partnership, which lasted the customary three
years.

In 1437 this partnership was dissolved. Giovenco d’Antonio withdrew, perhaps
because of ill health, for he died soon afterwards. A new partnership was formed
with three partners: the two remaining partners, Bernardo and his cousin, Giovenco
di Giuliano, and a new partner, none other than Giovanni di Bencini, the bookkeeper
in the earlier partnership. Bernardo invested 3075 florins, Giovenco di Giuliano
425 florins, and Giovanni Bencini 500 florins, making a total of 4000 florins, the same
amount of capital as in the preceding partnership. Both Giovenco and Giovanni
Bencini were active partners; Giovanni continued to keep the books.®

The division of profits was to be as follows: Bernardo was to draw on the basis
of £.2325, instead of £.3075 which he invested; Giovenco was to draw for £.1000,
instead of f.425, and Giovanni Bencini, for f.675, in place of £.500.°

For monthly drawing accounts, Bernardo was permitted to have 9% florins,
Giovenco 4 florins, and Giovanni 23 florins. If any partner overdrew his allowance,

The articles of association for this partnership between Bernardo d’Antonio as
silent partner and Giovenco di Giuliano and Giovanni di Bencini as active partners
provided that, if no partner desired to dissolve the partnership at the end of the
three-year period, it was to be automatically renewed for two years and then for two
more, and so on, until one partner expressed a desire to withdraw at least six months
in advance of the date for renewal, or unless one partner died.*

This partnership continued for a period of over twenty years with the same
capital of 4000 florins. It was terminated by the death of Giovanni Bencini in 1460.
Whether during the long duration of the partnership, the renewals were usually for
the period of two years provided for in the partnership agreement of 1437 or whether
new articles of association were occasionally drawn up is not clear because there is
no extant account book, nor are there partnership agreements for the years 1437 to
1458. In 1458 the partnership was renewed for three years by means of a new
contract which differs from the one of 1437 only in the shares of profit and the final
division of the partnership assets. The share of capital contributed by each partner
remained the same: f.3075 for Bernardo, f.425 for Giovenco, and f.500 for Bencini.
The latter was still the bookkeeper; Giovenco was still in charge of the manufacturing
and the selling of the cloth. The name of the partnership remained “Bernardo
d’Antonio and Company.”

The share of profits, according to the agreement of 1458, was 50% to Bernardo,
and 25% each to Giovenco and Giovanni.’ Giovenco was therefore receiving the
same return which he had received twenty years previous, Giovanni was receiving
more, that is to say, he was drawing on the basis of f.1000 instead of f.675, as in 1434,
and Bernardo was receiving a smaller share of the profits, drawing on the basis of
f.2000 instead of f.2325.

The active partners were still pledged not to engage in any other commercial
activities and Bernardo was still free to carry on, or to participate in, any business
ventures in or outside Florence.

We know from the Medici documents that Bernardo made use of this privilege,
but the information that the documents furnish is fragmentary and does not give a
complete picture of all his commercial activities during the thirty-odd years in which
his name appears in partnership agreements and account books.

The first additional partnership of which there is any record is one that Ber-
nardo formed in 1441. There were four partners: Averardo, Bernardo’s son, for
whom the new firm was to be named, Giovanni di Giovanni and Simone Istrada,

This partnership was not renewed when it expired in 1444. Instead, a new one

Bernardo himself, Averardo, his son, and Biagio d’Antonio, an outsider. The part-

lasted four years and was renewed for two more.* We do not know where the shop
of the first Averardo and Company partnership was located, but this second one was
across the river from the district of the shop of Bernardo d’Antonio and Company,
in the District of Via Maggio, or Oltrarno.

The subsidiary partnership probably served as an outlet for some of the goods
of the main partnership, although the subsidiary partnership carried on some man-
ufacturing itself.

The next partnership of which there is any record is one which Bernardo, in the
name of “Bernardo and Company,” formed with Giuliano di Giovenco di Giuliano,
the son of his cousin and partner, Giovenco di Giuliano. This partnership was
formed in 1458 at the same time as the renewed partnership between Bernardo,
Giovenco di Giuliano, and Giovanni Bencini. The name of the secondary partner-
ship was to be “Giuliano di Giovenco de’ Medici and Company” and the shop was to
be in the District of Via Maggio on the left bank of the Arno, possibly in the same
shop used by the earlier partnerships in the name of “Averardo di Bernardo and
Company.” The capital was 1400 florins, of which Bernardo and Company con-
tributed 1000 florins, and Giuliano di Giovenco 400 florins. Bernardo and Company
were to receive 55% of the profits (s.11 per lira), and Giuliano 45% (s.9 per lira).4
The articles of association were signed by all three partners of the firm of Bernardo
d’Antonio and.Company and by Giuliano.

permitted Giuliano to continue to supervise the affairs of the shop on the left bank

At the endof this partnership contract isanote to the effect that Bernardo died
in 1465, but that his sons Averardo and Lorenzo wished the partnership to continue
the full course of three years. It is therefore apparent from this and the example
above that the provision calling for the dissolution of a partnership on the death of
one of the partners was not always carried out. It was much more to the disadvant-
age of the silent partner to have a partnership which was making money dissolved
prematurely than it was to the active partners, because of the provision in most
fifteenth-century contracts—and in a number of fourteenth-century ones of Fran-
cesto Datini and others—providing for the division of all the assets of a partnership
on the same basis as the division of profits.

Because the active partners received no salary, it was customary for them to
receive a larger share of the profits than their capital contribution warranted. That
practice is clear to us, but the practice of dividing all the net assets on the same basis
as the profit, at the termination of the partnership, is somewhat confusing, according
to modern business standards. Unless the profits were large, the practice frequently
resulted in a loss of capital for the silent partner, although the active partner or
partners received a profit.

A concrete illustration of such a loss to a silent partner, when the balance sheet
showed a profit, is found in the “Secret Book” (Libro segreto, MS 502) for the part-
nership of Bernardo d’Antonio, Giovenco di Giuliano, and Giovanni Bencini, which
began in December 1458, and which was terminated in 1460 by the death of Bencini.
The “Secret Book” contained the account of the capital contributions of each part-
ner, his drawings, a summary of the final balance sheet copied from the ledger, and
the division of all the assets among the two living partners and the heirs of the
deceased one.

Folios 2 and 3 of the book show the contributions made by each partner in
stock and debtors from the preceding partnership, and in cash. Each partner
contributed approximately half in cash and half in assets from the preceding part-
nership:

partners on the basis of 50% and 25%, so that Bernardo received f.2520 s.12 d.4,

active partners, who had contributed only f.420 and f.500, received a good profit in
the final division of the partnership, but Bernardo, the silent partner, who had con-

have occurred very frequently, or Bernardo and other merchants, who made similar
partnership terms, would not have continued to form such combinations throughout
their lifetime.

I have found only one other instance of a capital loss to Bernardo at the end of a
partnership. It occurs in the final balance and division of assets! of the partnership
between Bernardo d’Antonio and Company and Giuliano di Giovenco, which lasted
from 1458 to 1461. It is interesting to note that in the succeeding partnership be-
tween Bernardo himself and Giuliano, for 1461-1464, the original capital of each part-
ner was to be returned to him and only the profits were to be divided on a percentage
basis.

For a Medici merchant with a more varied business career than that of Bernardo
d’Antonio, we must turn to Francesco di Giuliano di Giovenco di Giuliano, the grand-
son of Giovenco di Giuliano, who was Bernardo’s partner for over twenty years.
As far as I can tell from the Medici documents, Francesco began his business career
as a merchant dealing in jewels, jeweled belts, gold and silver ornaments, and other
objects of luxury. The oldest extant account book for this business is a journal
begun in 1476.2 During the year 1482, Francesco held the office of Chamberlain or
Treasurer of the town of Arezzo.? In March 1484, he formed a three-year partner-
ship with Gabriello Davicano for banking on a small scale (un traffico a uso di banco a
minuto) and for the sale of jewels, belts, etc., in which he had previously been dealing.
The capital was very small—600 florins, of which amount Francesco contributed 400
and Gabriello 200 florins. Francesco was to receive three-fifths of the profits and
Gabriello two-fifths. Neither partner was permitted to enter upon any other venture
during the three years of the partnership, but the contract does not state that Fran-
cesco had to give his services to the bank, as did Gabriello. The accounts were to be
inspected at least once every two months.4 Industrial and commercial partnership
agreements usually specified such an examination once a year.

The partnership with Davicano was continued until 1488, when Francesco
entered into a new banking partnership on a larger scale. The new partnership was
for five years, instead of the customary three years. There were three parties to the
contract, Francesco, Bastiano di Leonardo Buini, and Miniato Busini and Company.
The first two were the active partners and both their names appeared in the firm’s
name, which was “Francesco di Giuliano de’ Medici, Bastiano di Leonardo Buini
and Company.” The capital was 3000 florins, distributed as follows: Francesco con-
tributed f.800 in cash and his services were to be counted as f.200 more, making a total

2 MS 520.

4 Articles of Association, MS 495, pp. 40-41. Two ledgers for this partnership are extant,

of f.1000. Bastiano Buini contributed f.350 in cash and f.300 in repairs spent on the
bank building, and his person was valued at f.350, making a total of £.1000. The
silent partner, Miniato Buini and Company, invested f.1000 in cash. Each partner
was to receive one-third of the profits or losses. Francesco’s brother, Tommaso was
engaged as cashier.!

The banking partnership was apparently not renewed in 1493, at the end of the
five-year period. In 1491, before the termination of his activities as a banker, Fran-
cesco entered into a three-year partnership with his father and brother in the woolen-
cloth industry, in which Giuliano, the father, had been active for many years. The
father contributed 2000 florins, Francesco 700 florins, and Giovenco, his brother, 300
florins. Giovenco was in charge of the business. His father and brother were free
to engage in other enterprises. Giuliano was to share in $4 of the profits or loss
and of the final division of assets, Francesco in $$, and Giovenco in 3%.”

This partnership was evidently renewed for two years, and then in 1496 a larger
partnership in the woolen industry was formed for three years. There were five
partners: Giuliano di Giovenco, his sons Francesco and Giovenco, Alfieri di Istrinati,
and Niccold Carsidoni. The name of the partnership, as in the earlier one of 1491,
was “Giuliano di Giovenco and Francesco di Giuliano and Company.”

The capital was 5000 florins, divided as follows: Giuliano di Giovenco f.1700,
Francesco di Giuliano, Alfieri Istrinati, and Niccolò Carsidoni each f.1000, and
Giovenco di Giuliano f.300.4 Giovenco was to be the only active partner, so that he
was to receive a larger proportion of the profits than the partners who invested 1000
florins. Giovenco was to draw profits on the basis of s.3 d.10 per lira, his father on
the basis of s.5 d.11, and the remaining three partners were to draw for s.3 d.5 each.
Only the profits (or losses) were to be so divided. According to this partnership
contract the original amount of capital was to be returned to each partner unless
losses would not permit so doing.®

Niccold Carsidoni, who spent much of his time in the Levant, was to try to sell
most of the cloth produced by the company in Romania and Turkey, and was to
receive a commission for his services.®

Giuliano died in 1498. There is no evidence to show whether the partnership
was dissolved on account of his death or not.

The next trace of Francesco’s activities is found in a ledger of 1502-1505 for a
partnership in the woolen industry with Alfieri Istrinati and Alessandro Giudicci.”

During the same period Francesco was doing a considerable business inde-
pendently in the export of cloth. A set of books for the years 1503-1509, including a
letter book and a copybook of invoices and of carriage and shipping charges, show

that he was shipping cloth to Lyons, to Ragusa, to Adrianople, and to Pera. In
return he imported Brusa silks, wax, and pepper from the East, and wool from
France.!_ Most of the cloth he exported was purchased from the industrial partner-
ship with Istrinati and Giudicci and from another industrial partnership formed in
1506 between Francesco, his brother Giovanni, Niccolò Michelozzi, and Giovanni
Maringhi, who lived in Pera.”

In 1508 Francesco entered into a partnership for the dyeing of cloth—this time
with two of his brothers, Giovanni, who was in the above-mentioned partnership for
the manufacture of cloth, and Giovenco, and with Bartolomeo Bernini and Giovanni
di Rudolfo di Franco, both of them master dyers. The name of the firm was to be
“Giovenco e Giovanni di Giuliano and Company.” The capital was 800 florins.
Francesco invested f.200, Giovenco the same amount, Giovanni de’ Medici f.300,
Bartolomeo Bernini f.100, and Giovanni di Franco gave only his services. The
latter two were in charge of the dyehouse.’

Bartolomeo Bernini, who contributed one-eighth of the capital, was to receive
one-fifth of the profits, and Giovanni di Franco, who contributed no capital, was to
to receive approximately one-sixth of the profits. At the termination of the partner-
ship the original share of capital was to be returned to each contributing partner, so
that Bernini would not receive more than the 100 florins he had invested and Gio-
vanni di Franco would not receive any capital This arrangement for dividing
assets and profits at the dissolution of a company differs from the practice, common in
the fifteenth century, of giving the active partners the same share of the total assets
as their percentage of the profits.

There are no extant account books for this company of dyers, nor any evidence
to show whether it was renewed or not.

During Francesco’s later years (he died between 1525 and 1530), he continued
to give his personal services to his private business of exporting cloth, assisted by his
son Raffaello.® And he continued to contribute funds to partnerships as a silent
partner.

The last partnerships formed by Francesco of which there is any record were
industrial ones, for the manufacture of cloth, formed in 1513, 1521, and 1525. In
each case there was only one other partner, and although in all three partnerships,
the name of the firm was that of Francesco’s son, ‘Raffaello di Francesco de’ Medici
and Company,” Raffaello himself does not appear as a partner, either silent or
active, in any of them. But in all three he was to keep the general ledger and take
care of the correspondence, at a salary of two florins per month. As his father’s
procurator, he could also give advice and orders. The first of these partnerships was
one between Francesco and Antonio Bartoli with a capital of £.5426 s.13 d.4, of
which Francesco contributed f.4760. Antonio was credited with a capital contribu-

tion of £.666 s.13 d.4, of which only f.250 was in cash. The balance of f.416 s.13 d.4
was the estimate for his personal services as the only active partner. The profits
were to be divided on a percentage, based on the share of each partner in the com-
pany—approximately 88% to Francesco and 12% to Antonio Bartoli! This part-
nership was evidently extended at the end of the three-year period, in 1516. In 1521
it was renewed with a change in the amount of the capital, so that new articles of
association were drawn up. The total of the capital was raised to 6250 florins, of
which Francesco contributed 5000 florins, and Antonio Bartoli 400 florins in cash and
850 florins as the estimated value of his services. Francesco was to receive four-
fifths of the profits and Bartoli one-fifth When this partnership expired in Decem-
ber 1524, it was not renewed.

A few months later, Francesco de’ Medici formed a partnership with Bernardo
Baglioni to continue the manufacture of cloth under the name of “Raffaello di
Francesco de’ Medici and Company.” As in the earlier partnerships with Antonio
Bartoli, Raffaello was not one of the partners, but was in charge of the main ledger
and the correspondence. The terms of the partnership agreement are similar to the
preceding ones. Francesco contributed 4000 florins out of a capital of 4900 florins;
Baglioni gave 200 florins in cash and was allowed 700 florins for his services, so that
his share of the capital was fixed at 900 florins, and his share of the profits at approxi-
mately one-fifth.*

The terms of these last three partnership agreements regarding capital and profit
illustrate the method of remunerating an active partner who received no salary for
his services which is most frequently found inthe Medici articles of association of the
sixteenth century. This method differs from that most common in the fifteenth
century, and from that found in the partnership for dyeing in 1508.

In the fifteenth century active partners were usually rewarded by receiving a
larger share of the profits, throughout the partnership, than the percentage of their
contribution to the capital of the company called for, and by receiving that same
larger proportion of the total assets at the termination of a partnership. In the
partnership of 1508, the active partner, who contributed some capital, received
a larger percentage of the profits only than the percentage of his investment would
call for, that is, he received one-fifth of the profits for one-eighth of the capital. At
the dissolution of the partnership, he was to receive his original capital of 100 florins
plus one-fifth of the profits. The partner who contributed services only was to be
rewarded by one-sixth of the profits.

In the partnership of 1513 the active partner was to be rewarded, not by a larger
percentage of profits or of total assets, but by having his services evaluated in terms
of money, and by having the monetary value of his person added to the cash he
contributed to form his share of the capital of the partnership. The percentage of the
profits he was to receive corresponded exactly to the total figure for his contribution
of capital. In other words, Antonio Franco, who contributed f.250 in cash and whose

1 Articles of Association, MS 495, pp. 76-79.
2 Ibid., pp. 73 f.
8 Ibid., pp. 92-96.

MEDICI PARTNERSHIPS 347

person was valued at an additional f.416 s.13 d.4, making a total of f.666 s.13 d.4 as his
share of the original capital of the partnership with Francesco de’ Medici, or approxi-
mately 12% of the entire partnership capital of f.5426 s.13 d.4, was to receive 12% of
all the profits, and at the end of the partnership would receive f.666 s.13 d.4 in cash,
stock, and debtors—the amount of capital he was supposed to have contributed.

To summarize, the Medici partnerships of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries
furnish interesting illustrations of the concept of ability as capital, comparable to the
modern practice of giving a new partner, when he enters a firm, a number of shares of
stock or of crediting him with capital which he has not actually contributed in any
material form. In the fifteenth century, preferred treatment given to active part-
ners who contributed some capital was either in the form of: (1) a preferred share of
the profits, or (2) a preferred share of profits and assets on distribution. This second
arrangement is characteristic of most fifteenth-century partnerships. It sometimes
resulted in a heavy loss to the silent partner, in a partnership of short duration,
even though the balance sheet showed a profit.

In the sixteenth century an active partner who contributed a small amount of
cash was usually credited with a share of the capital two or three times as large as his
actual contribution. His share of the profits would correspond to the total share of
capital with which he was credited.

In the case of a partner who contributed only his person and no capital, the
partner received a share of the profits for his services. He would likewise have to
share in a loss on the same basis as he was to share in the profits.

The Medici partnerships of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries were all part-
nerships with full liability. In the seventeenth-century articles of association found
in MS 495, there are examples of partnerships with limited liability, that is, partner-
ships in which the active partners and any silent partners whose names appeared in
the title of the firm had full liability and other silent partners were liable only for the
amount of their contribution to the capital of the partnership. The earliest example
in the Medici documents is a partnership formed in 1681 to manufacture silk cloth.
There were two active partners, with full liability, and six silent partners with limited
liability.t

1 MS 495, pp. 162-187.

APPENDIX II
MEDICI METHODS OF BOOKKEEPING

In his treatise on bookkeeping, published in Venice in 1494, Luca Paciolo
describes a system of double-entry bookkeeping based upon the use of three books.
The first was the memorial or wastebook: a general book of primary entry in which
every transaction was to be entered as it occurred and with figures in the monetary
unit used in the transaction. Before being transferred to the journal, each entry in
the wastebook was to be changed into a uniform monetary unit. The journal differed
from modern ones in having only one effective column for the monetary figures of
both debit and credit entries. From the journal, entries were posted to the ledger.

The system Paciolo described in such minute detail must have been fully
developed long before he wrote about it. An earlier treatise of double-entry book-
keeping describing three books was apparently written by Benedetto Cotrugli of
Ragusa about 1463, although the manuscript was not printed until 1573.

The oldest-known example of double-entry bookkeeping is the Genoese com-
munal stewards account book of 1340, which is written in Latin. It shows a fully
developed system of double-entry with debits and credits opposite each other real
accounts for goods, and a Profit and Loss account. Double-entry was used in the
Datini ledgers as early as 1383.1 For Florence the oldest ledger kept in correct
double-entry form of which we know is one that belonged to Averardo de’ Medici
and Co., money-changers or bankers in Florence, for the year 1395.

The earliest Venetian ledger with double-entry, belonged to the Soranzo Bros.,
bankers, and covers the period 1406-1434. Another early Venetian ledger is that of
the Barbarigo firm for the years 1430-1444.

Bearing in mind the fact that double-entry bookkeeping was used in Genoa,
Prato, Florence, and probably Venice before 1400 (apparently not the system of three
books described by Cotrugli and Paciolo but a simpler one in which a ledger and
possibly a wastebook were used without any journal), let us examine the Selfridge
Collection of Medici Manuscripts of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries for the light
they may shed upon an intermediate period in the history and methods of double-
entry bookkeeping. In the Datini account books of the second half of the fourteenth
century the gradual transition from paragraph accounting? to double-entry book-

1 Corsani, G., I fondaci ei banchi di un mercante pratese del trecento, pp. 82 Î.

2 Paragraph or diary accounting, in which each entry is described in paragraph form, was the
earliest form of bookkeeping. Out of it gradually developed double-entry bookkeeping, in which
system the wastebook and sometimes the journal were still kept in paragraph form. ‘‘Single-entry”
is frequently applied to all examples of bookkeeping which were not kept in correct double-entry form,
but, strictly speaking, single-entry bookkeeping is a definite’ system which was not introduced until
the eighteenth century.

keeping can easily be traced.! In the Medici account books of the succeeding fifty
years—that is, the first half of the fifteenth century—the same gradual transition
manifests itself, although less clearly than in the Datini records, because fewer Medici
volumes are extant.

It is an interesting, although not surprising, phenomenon that the transition
stage from one form of bookkeeping to another illustrated by the books of the famous
Pratese merchant, Francesco da Marco Datini, and by those of some of the Medici
during the latter part of the fourteenth century, is repeated again fifty years later in
the books of another branch of the Medici House of Florence.

The oldest account book in the Selfridge Collection, MS 492, is a small volume
with entries from 1406 to 1418. It is entitled “Book in which I shall write debtors
and creditors” (libro in sul quale iscriverré debitori e creditori). In this Giovenco di
Giuliano, a factor for the cloth manufacturers Lorenzo d’Andrea di Messer Ugo and
company, recorded his dealings with spinners and weavers, payments for various
commodities, and the money he owed to the company from his collections. The
book is a typical example of paragraph accounting. There is some attempt at classi-
fication of accounts by the separation of debit and credit entries—the credit entries
being placed in the first half of the book and the debit entries in the second half.
The credit entries are for sums owed to Lorenzo d’Andrea and Company and to others,
and for amounts due Giovenco de’ Medici for his services. The debit entries are
chiefly for advances made to women spinners with the record of the repayments
which were made either in money or in work, or in both.

debits facing credits on opposite pages, but it has no impersonal accounts, no postings
from other books, and no final balance at the end of the book.

The next account book in point of time is a ledger for 1431-1434, MS 496,
from a partnership in the woolen industry between Giovenco di Giuliano and his
cousin Giovenco d’Antonio. It is a large folio volume, 11} inches by 16 inches,
entitled “Book of Debtors and Creditors” (libri debitori e creditori), the usual title
for double-entry ledgers among the Medici Manuscripts. Not until 1442 is any other
name used, and from then on only occasionally. Practically all the Medici ledgers
relating to the woolen cloth industry, the cloth trade, or banking, of both the fifteenth
and sixteenth centuries, are the same size as this.

This ledger is not in correct double-entry form with debits opposite credits,
but it is an example of a transitional stage between paragraph accounting and double-
entry bookkeeping. In the first part are listed the personal accounts of debtors to
the partnership, with the credits for these debit entries, i.e., partial or full payment
of the amounts due, given below the debits on the same page. Two to four accounts
are on the same page, and, as the space allotted to each account is therefore rather
limited, the accounts are frequently transferred to other pages. Each account which
has been transferred or closed has one or two diagonal lines running through it from
right to left. (This is also characteristic of the earlier account books, MSS 492 and
493). Besides the personal accounts in the Debit section of the book, there is a
Profit and Loss account (foll. 19", 25") in this section. In the second half of the
ledger are listed the accounts with creditors of the company. The amounts owed to
the creditors are given first, below them, the payments made, or the debits. The
accounts of the capital invested by both partners are also in this section.

In the Debit section, dé or deono dare is followed by Ane or Annone dato. In
the Credit section dé or deono avere is followed by Ane auto.

On fol. 27” the names of the debtors and the amounts due them are listed in
summary form, one below the other. From the total of these accounts receivable,
f.819 s.21, is deducted the total of the accounts payable, summarized on fol. 587,
including the capital invested by the two partners, less their drawings, which is con-
sidered as a credit owed by the firm to the partners. The sum of f.699 s.24 d.7
resulting from this subtraction is the profit which is divided between the partners on
the basis of two-thirds to Giovenco d’Antonio, whose original capital investment was
1000 florins, and one-third to Giovenco di Giuliano, whose capital investment was
only 300 florins. Both were active partners. On fol. 29" is given a summary of the
division of all the accounts receivable between the two partners on the basis of one-
third and two-thirds. The creditors were to be paid by the two partners separately,
each one receiving a group of creditors, including themselves as creditors for the
remainder of their capital (fol. 58"). Thus the ledger was balanced out and closed.

In these three account books then, MSS 492, 493, 496, dating from 1406 to 1434,
and belonging to one man, we can examine different phases in the gradual transition
from paragraph accounting to an incomplete system of double-entry bookkeeping.
The first and third manuscripts, 492 and 496, resemble each other more than they
do the intermediate one, possibly because both are examples of accounts belonging
to business partnerships in the woolen cloth industry, whereas MS 493 is a personal
ledger, containing accounts of private income from such sources as leases, sales and
purchase of country produce, etc. In this personal ledger of 1417-1428 we find in
use the so-called “Venetian system” of placing debits opposite credits, the debits
always on the left-hand page, and the credits on the right-hand page. Accounts are
cancelled when they balance, either because full payment has been made or because
the account has been balanced by adding an entry providing for the transfer of the
account toanother page. But aside from these two characteristic features of double-
entry, none of the other characteristics of a well-developed double-entry system

1 Medici MS 496, fol. 26".
2 Ibid., fol. 56".

354 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

appears in this volume; for example, there are no references to corresponding books,
such as a journal or cash book, nor are there references to the ledger folios where the
counterpart of each debit and credit may be found, because all the accounts are
accounts with persons. Lastly, the book contains no closing balance.

I have called MS 492, 1406-1418 an example of paragraph accounting and MS
Ledger 496, 1431-1434 an example of a transitional stage in accounting, although the
entries in the two books are in the same narrative form; that is to say, debits and
credits are given one below the other instead of opposite, with the debits sometimes
above the credit entries of a given account and the credits sometimes above the debit
entries of another account, depending upon whether the original entry is for an
account receivable or an account payable.

The fact that debit entries such as those reproduced above—the account with
Caterina di Ciobo from MS 492 and with Francesco and Filippo Portinari from MS
496—have corresponding credit entries on the same page, so that each account could
be and was usually balanced, meant that some of the fundamentals of double-entry
bookkeeping, namely orderly grouping of entries and facility of balancing, were
present in these early account books, although the placing of credit and debit entries
below one another did not make it as easy to examine the state of an account as did
the double-entry method of debits on the left and credits on the right.

In contrast to the similarity between MSS 492 and 496 in placing debtors in
one-half of the book and creditors in the other half, and in placing their corresponding
credits and debits below the accounts instead of opposite them, there are very im-
portant differences between the two volumes. That is, MS 496 shows much more
progress in the direction of double-entry bookkeeping, and except for the fact that
the personal ledger, MS 493, has debits opposite credits, MS 496 also shows improve-
ment over that ledger in bookkeeping technic.

MSS 492 and 493 do not refer to any corresponding account books, nor to the
ledger folios for the counterparts of each debit and credit entry, and have no imper-
sonal accounts nor any balance.

On the other hand MS Ledger 496 has all of these characteristics of double-entry
bookkeeping. First, each entry is posted from another book to which a page refer-
ence is given. The most important of these books, the one from which most ledger
entries are posted, is neither of the two books of primary entry described by Paciolo—
the wastebook and the journal—but a stock book or book of purchases and sales
(libro compere e vendite), which differs from the early journals principally in having a
more orderly arrangement of entries than do the journals, purchases and sales being
separated and entered in different sections of the book, instead of being entered
together without any attempt at classification as in the journals. That account
books called journals (giornale) were in use before the middle of the fifteenth century,
we know from references found in another early Medici ledger, MS 498, 1441 (0.S.)-
1444 (0.s.), to journals kept by customers of the Medici, particularly silk merchants
and soap-manufacturers. Daybooks or wastebooks, called memoriali and straccia-
fogli, belonging to customers, are also referred to in MS Ledger 498.

No wastebook belonging to the Medici merchants is referred to in MSS Ledgers
496 or 498, but the omission of any reference to such a book of primary entry in these

MEDICI METHODS OF BOOKKEEPING 855

ledgers does not preclude its use, because in the later sets of Medici account books, in
which wastebooks as well as journals are found, the corresponding ledgers never con-
tain references to the wastebooks, even when entries are posted directly from the
wastebook to the ledger without passing through the journal.

Cash entries in MS Ledger 496 were posted either from the book of Income and
Outgo (entrata e uscita) or from the Cash book (quaderno di cassa). We have numer-
ous examples of books of income and outgo, but not a single cash book is extant in the
Selfridge Collection.

One other book is referred to in our ledger, namely, a book of dyers and work-
men (libro tintori e lavoranti), a special journal or memorandum book of wages due to
workmen which records the amount of material given to them to work upon (if they
were not in a central workshop), the dates when it was returned, and the wages due
them. The amounts owed for wages were then transferred to the personal accounts
of the workmen in the ledger. Posting entries directly from a cash book and from a
special journal to a ledger are supposed to be modern practices, yet are found in use
in the middle of the fifteenth century. Memorandum books of wages are also found
in the Datini Manuscripts of the fourteenth century.

We find, then, as early as 1431 a rather complex set of books in use in industrial
partnerships—and it should be stated here that the account books described in the
following pages relate, unless otherwise specified, to the Medici as industrial entre-
preneurs, as manufacturers of woolen cloth. The books used by the Medici as
dyers of cloth differ only slightly, while the sets of books used in the cloth trade (when
that trade was separated from manufacturing) and in banking differ considerably
from those used by the industrial entrepreneurs in the woolen industry. These three
groups will be described later. The books used by the Medici cloth manufacturers
in 1431 and throughout the fifteenth century were: a stock book (which was essen-
tially a journal), a ledger, a cash book, a book of income and outgo, and a wage book
for workmen and dyers. Their relationship may be illustrated by a diagram:

In the last quarter of the fifteenth century the wage book was divided into two
books—one for memoranda of work given out to spinners, warpers, and weavers,
Libro dei filatori e tessitori (first mentioned in MS Ledger 510, 1482-1486); the other
one for dyers and all other workmen, which retained the name of Libro tintori e
lavoranti.

The oldest extant Medici journal dates from 1476, but is a record of personal
expenses. The other fifteenth-century Medici journals belonged to banking partner-
ships and to a firm of dyers. Only from 1503 on are there journals for wool-manu-

356 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

facturing. The oldest extant wastebook (memoriale) in the Collection is from 1493.
Whether there were earlier Medici wastebooks we cannot tell, because the few
journals which are prior to that date do not mention any book of primary entry, and
the ledgers would never mention wastebooks.

Let us return to thesubject of the characteristics of MS Ledger 496. Besides the
references to entries in other books and to the carrying forward of accounts from one
ledger-folio to another, and of references to counterpart accounts when payments
were made in the name of a third party, of which examples are given on the two
ledger-pages reproduced above (foll. 1", 50”), there are a few references to ledger folios
for the counterparts of certain debit and credit entries, especially under the Profit and
Loss account, foll. 19", 25". The practice of giving the ledger page reference for the
counterpart of each entry in the ledger is not consistently used for every entry in the
Medici ledgers until 1482; before that such information is only occasionally given,
as in this ledger.

Of impersonal accounts MS Ledger 496 has only two: a petty expense account
for the shop (spese minute di bottega) in which there are numerous debits posted from
the cash book with no explanation of their use and one entry for cloth for a hanging
in the doorway of theshop. The credit entries below the debit ones are for discounts
paid on exchange. The balance of the expense account is posted to the other nominal
account—Profit and Loss. The latter account is not used as extensively in this
ledger as in later ones, especially in those of the sixteenth century, when practically
all ventures are closed into it. In MS 496 we find Profit and Loss debited for petty
expenses; for interest on money loaned to the partnership by an outsider, Bernardo
d’Antonio, brother of one of the partners and cousin of the other; and for the account
books and paper used in the partnership. Profit and Loss is credited with premiums
on exchange, and with small sums paid to dyers and others to balance their accounts
in this ledger.

The closing of MS Ledger 496 has been described above, pages 8 f. The balance
sheet is very simple, and lacks some of the characteristics of later balance sheets, such
as an inventory of stock and fixtures and the listing of the capital accounts of the
partners as separate items under liabilities instead of their inclusion in the accounts
payable, as is done here.

It should be recalled, however, that this ledger represents a transitional or
early stage in the development of double-entry bookkeeping. It has many charac-
teristics of double-entry bookkeeping in a rudimentary form, although it lacks the
most outstanding feature, namely, the placing of debits on the left and credits on the
right facing each other, and has, to a limited extent only, the fundamental charac-
teristic of double-entry, that is the making of two entries for each transaction, one
debit and one credit.

The oldest Medici ledger, M.S 498, which combines all these features of double-
entry bookkeeping, was begun just ten years after the above-described ledger.
Like many of the Medici ledgers, it, too, is for a partnership lasting three years, from
1441 (0.5.) to 1444 (0.s.). The debits are on the left-hand and the credits on the
right-hand pages. There is a Profit and Loss account, but no other impersonal one.

358 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

As in the earlier ledger, a final balance was made when the book was closed and, as
the partnership ended at the same time, the profits and the capital in the form of
stock, fixtures, and accounts receivable were divided among the three partners.

This balance (saldo) of February 1444 (0.s.), is the first complete balance sheet
in the ledgers. It is the model for those in the succeeding Medici ledgers of the
fifteenth century. All the stock—consisting of cloth, wool, and dyestuffs, and the
fixtures are inventoried (fol. 81%) and below them ‘the accounts receivable are listed
(foll. 81%, 827). Cash on hand is not included in this or any later balance sheet.
Instead, on the date of the final balance or a few days previous, the cash was dis-
tributed among the partners, their accounts being debited for drawings of cash (MS
498) or for cash with which to settle the accounts payable (MS 501). The total of
the stock, fixtures, and debtors gives the total Assets. The Liabilities consisting of
creditors (listed on fol. 82”) and the capital contributed by the partners are deducted
from the total Assets (fol. 82"). The result of the subtraction is the profit (or loss).
The profit is divided among the partners according to a percentage provided for in
the partnership agreement. A list of seven bad debts is given on fol. 83” and the
seven debtors are divided among the three partners on the basis of one-half and one-
fourth as for the profits. These lost accounts do not appear on the balance sheet.
In this balance the silent partner, Bernardo de’ Medici, who invested four-fifths of
the capital but gave no services, received one-half of the profits, and the two active
partners, whose share of the capital was one-sixth and one-thirtieth, received each
one-fourth of the profits.

We see at a glance that Bernardo, the silent partner, did not receive his full
share of the capital plus profit, and that the other two partners received more than
their share. What evidently happened was that not only the profit but the capital
as well was divided approximately on the basis of one-half to Bernardo, the silent
partner, and one-fourth to each of the active partners. This practice of dividing the
capital at the end of a partnership, not on the basis of each partner’s original contri-
bution, but on the basis of the division of profit and loss, is common in partnerships
between active and silent partners during the Middle Ages and is provided for in the
articles of association of such partnerships. For a further discussion of this practice
see Appendix I, p. 342.

In describing the balance sheet of 1444 in MS Ledger 498 we are dealing with
one that is, with very few exceptions, typical of the balances in the Medici ledgers
from that date until the end of the fifteenth century. From 1460 (0.s.) on, the final
accounts for the partners, which in M.S 498 have the debits written below the credits
(see the excerpt from fol. 83" given above), are in correct double-entry form with the
debits, i.e., the amounts they received at the dissolution of the partnership or the
closing of the books, on the left-hand page opposite the credits, i.e., the amounts due
them for capital and profit.

In some of the balance sheets accounts payable are not listed, because enough
cash to pay them has been debited to the partners’ drawing accounts on the day that
the books were closed. In MS Ledger 501 there was enough cash on hand to pay
fifteen out of the seventeen accounts payable, so that one of the partners was debited
with cash to pay the fifteen creditors and only the two remaining creditors appear on
the balance sheet of 24 March 1460 (0.5.)

362 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

The division of bad debts which appears in MS 498 is not found in many of the
ledgers. More common is the practice of listing cloth in the hands of agents abroad
and not included in the stock inventory. For example, in the balance sheet of 24
March 1460 (0.s.), in MS Ledger 501 there is a note to the effect that certain cloths
have not been included in the inventory of stock. These cloths which are in the
hands of agents in Palermo and the Levant are listed on the pages following the final
account of the partners, foll. 50-52". The money for them was to be divided
between the partners whenever it was received. These accounts for cloth in the
hands of agents were continued during 1461, until all the outstanding cloth was sold
and the returns therefrom were divided between the two partners.

Thus far, we have described only the balancing and closing of ledgers at the
termination of a partnership, when all the assets were divided among the partners,
even though the partnership was soon renewed or a new one between the same
partners was formed. Most of the final balance sheets found in the fifteenth-century
Medici ledgers are of this type.

Although all the extant Medici partnership agreements provided for an annual
distribution of profit (or loss), we find no record of balances made during the term of
a partnership, which was usually three years, with the exception of two ledgers—
MS 499, 1444-50 with balance sheets (saldi) for 1448 and 1450, and MS 504, 1461-
64 with balance sheets of 31 January 1462 (0.s.), and 12 March 1464 (0.s.). The
balances of 1448 and 1462 in the two ledgers are almost identical in form. They
differ from the final balances only in that the accounts receivable and payable, in-
stead of being divided between the partners, were posted to a joint partnership
account and from there the accounts receivable were carried forward. Since the
partnerships were to continue, the capital and profit, less the drawings, were turned
back into the business with the opening of new capital accounts.

There is one other kind of account book besides the general ledgers which should
be mentioned in connection with balance sheets. It is the Libro segreto, “secret book”,
or private ledger, of which only two examples are extant in the Selfridge Collection.
The first one, MS 502, is for the years 1458-1460 (o0.s.), and the second, MS 568 (1),
for 1496-1498. The first is complete, the second is not.

These books, both small-sized and thin (83 inches by 114 inches), contain the
capital accounts of the partners (three in the first book, five in the second); their
drawing accounts; the final balance sheet of the partnership with all that went to
make it up, i.e., the inventory of stock and fixtures, accounts receivable and accounts
payable, and the division of net assets among the partners. All this information
may be found in the general ledger of the fifteenth century, but it is more compact
and more easily examined in the small private ledger than in the main ledger, where
the capital and drawing accounts are likely to be scattered through a number of
pages.

How common the practice of keeping a “secret book” was among the Medici
merchants we do not know because there are only two in this collection and because
they are never referred to in any other account books. This silence may be inter-
preted in either of two ways. First, that if a private ledger were included in each set
of books belonging to a partnership some reference to such a book should exist

MEDICI METHODS OF BOOKKEEPING 363

somewhere in the Medici Manuscripts. Absence of any reference might lead to the
conclusion that the practice of keeping a secret book was not common. Thus far,
no reference to one has been found, even in the itemized account for the purchase of a
complete set of books for a new partnership beginning in 1490 found in MS Ledger
513 (fol. 24"), and which includes even an index to the general ledger (quadernuccio
cogli stratti). But no libro segretois mentioned. Secondly, that the title and nature
of the secret book precluded reference to it or mention of it in the regular account
books, but that it may have been in fairly common use by the Medici of the fifteenth
century, as we know it was by the Bardi, Peruzzi, Datini, and other companies of the
fourteenth century, especially before double-entry bookkeeping was introduced.

Before we leave the subject of final balances in the Medici ledgers, attention
should be called to the fact that, whereas almost every fifteenth-century ledger has a
balance sheet, not a single one exists in any of the sixteenth-century Medici ledgers.
In many of these later ledgers the last pages have been torn out, but the four which
are intact contain no trace of a balance sheet such as are found in the earlier ledgers.
When we turn to the accounts of the partners in these four sixteenth-century ledgers,
however, we find in each case that a profit was divided among them. Therefore,
these ledgers must have been balanced and closed. In two instances the counterpart
for the profit entry in each partner’s account is found in the Profit and Loss account
and in the other two books it is found in the Cloth account. The two Profit and Loss
accounts show that the profit is posted from the Cloth account, so that in all four
ledgers the tracing of the profit entries leads back to the account called Panni lavorati
e finiti (Cloth manufactured and sold) or sometimes shortened to Panni finiti. In
each ledger numerous pages throughout the ledger are devoted to this account of all
the cloth manufactured by each partnership. On the last pages of these cloth
accounts is found a statement drawn up to show the profit on all the cloth that has
been sold, a statement which serves the same purpose as the fifteenth-century balance
sheets. On the debit side of each cloth account are the following items: (1) the
sum total of all the wool purchased and used in the making of cloth during the period
of the partnership, (2) the total amount spent for dyestuffs and the dyeing of wool and
cloth, and (3) the total of all the other manufacturing costs—wages, materials used
by the workmen such as oil, combs, cards, and teasels, and miscellaneous expenses.
The total of the debit side shows the cost of producing the finished cloth. On the
credit side of the account appears a summary of all the cloth sold with the total
receipts from all the sales. 300 to 370 full-length cloths were manufactured and sold
by each partnership. Apparently no cloth remained unsold, but in some of the
ledgers much of it was sold to the individual partners. Nor were there any out-
standing accounts payable or receivable. All had been balanced through the use of
the Profit and Loss account. Therefore the difference between the Debit and the
Credit side of the Cloth accounts in the four ledgers represented the total net profit
of the companies.

In the two earlier ledgers, MS 554 (6), 1530-1534, and MS 558 (1), 1534-1544,
after the profit has been determined, the cloth account is balanced by dividing the
profit among the three partners on the debit side of the account and posting from

In the two later ledgers, MS 560 (3), 1547-1556, and MS 567 (8), 1556-1559,
the Cloth account is balanced by posting the profit to the credit side of the Profit and
Loss account. Then on the debit side of the Profit and Loss account the division of
profit is made among the partners pro rata, and posted to their individual accounts.

In the two earlier ledgers the Profit and Loss accounts have only small amounts
posted to them. The amounts are posted from personal accounts which did not quite
balance until a Profit and Loss entry, frequently for only a few denari or soldi, was
added on one side or the other of the accounts in order to balance them. The coun-
terparts of such entries were posted to Profit and Loss. No impersonal accounts
appear in these Profit and Loss accounts, with the exception of a small entry posted
from the Cloth account in MS Ledger 554 (6).

The Profit and Loss accounts in the two later ledgers are much more detailed.
Numerous impersonal, as well as personal, accounts are closed into Profit and Loss,
including the profit from the Cloth accounts and an Alms account of one percent of
the profit, Limosine si debbeno dare a distribuire per Vamore di Dio per questa ragione
(Alms which must be given to be distributed for the love of God for this company),
found in MS 560 (3). Cash accounts are also posted to Profit and Loss. The
fifteenth-century ledgers had no cash accounts, only separate cash books. The
sixteenth-century companies used both. Since no cash books are extant, we cannot
compare the cash accounts with the cash books to see the relation between the two.

From 1520 on, two new accounts appear in all the general industrial ledgers—
one called Quaderno di nostri manifattori (ledger of our workmén) and the other called
Manifatture di nostra ragione (manufactures, or cost of manufacturing of our com-
pany)—both of which refer to a new type of account book, a special ledger for wages
paid to workmen, apparently the only new book added to the set of industrial books
used by the Medici in the sixteenth century, if we overlook the fact that in this later
century the special journal or memorandum book of wages due to spinners, warpers,
and weavers (libro tessitori e filatori) are frequently divided into two separate books—
one for spinners (libro filatori) and one for warpers and weavers (libro tessitori).

The special wage ledger will receive further treatment in connection with the
special wage journals.

The sixteenth-century ledgers furnish a number of examples of the use of the
term “current account” (conto corrente) and one interesting example of “time
account” (conto di tempi). Ceccherelli illustrates the use of both terms in a business
ledger of 1459 belonging to Piero and Giovanni, sons of Cosimo de’ Medici! The
current and time accounts in this fifteenth-century ledger were kept with bankers
and Medici branch-houses. These terms are similarly used in the sixteenth-century
Medici books of the Selfridge Collection. The current accounts are for partners and

1 Ceccherelli, A., I libri di mercatura della Banca Medici, pp. 59 ff.

368 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

bankers. The only time account found thus far is with a firm of bankers and wool
importers, Alessandro di Niccolò Antinori and Co. There is also a current account
with them, both in MS Ledger 560 (3), 1547-1556. In the time account (foll. 1-2"),
Antinori and Co. are credited with sales of wool made to the Medici on time, usually
one year. On the debit side appear entries recording time payments to be paid to
the bankers by Medici customers for cloth they had purchased on time, usually with
terms of one year. These payments may have been made by bank transfers of credit.
In the current account (foll. 26-27") Antinori and Co. are credited with sums of
money they handed over to Alessandro Catastini, the Medici cashier, and they are
debited with amounts paid to them in cash by Medici debtors on behalf of the

Medici.

Before leaving the subject of general ledgers we should say something more
regarding their names. At least two-thirds of the sixty-two ledgers in the Selfridge
Collection are called Libro debitori e creditori (book of debtors and creditors). A
very few are called Libro grande (large book). The remainder are called after the
color of their leather covers—white book, red book, blue book, yellow book, green
book, purple book, etc. The colored books are almost all of the sixteenth century,
most of the fifteenth-century ledgers having parchment covers of natural hue,
reenforced with three to five leather straps.

In the journals and other books the ledgers are referred to by their titles, with
the frequent addition of the letter which was used to distinguish all the books of a
given set and which usually appeared on the cover of parchment-bound books and on
the title-page of leather-bound books. Thus in a journal with the cover marked A
there might be references toa ledger entitled Libro bianco segno A (white book marked
A).

Every Medici ledger may have had an index (stratto). Many are extant from

both centuries. That not more indexes have come down to us is easily explained by
the fact that they are always in separate books, usually as long as the ledger, but
only half as wide, bound in sheets of parchment; and that very few of them were
labelled in any way to, identify them with their corresponding ledgers in case they
became separated from them. Indeed, there are several indexes in the Medici Collec-
tion as yet unidentified, because they have fallen out of their places between the
front cover and the title-page of their ledgers. The indexes have thumb-initials
like a modern dictionary, except that they are usually very artistic in design and
colored or illuminated. ‘The names of persons are not entered under the last name
but under the first; for example, Giuliano de’ Medici is always listed under G, not
M. There is no attempt to alphabetize under each initial, although Paciolo recom-
mends such a practice. The impersonal accounts are listed under the first words,
as in the case of personal ones; for example, Avanzi e Disavanzi is under A as we
should expect, but Una Mandata di panni is under U, not under M or P, where we
might place it.

The book of primary entry used throughout the fifteenth century by the Medici
in their industrial partnerships was the Stock Book, called Libro compere e vendite e
ricordanze (book of purchases and sales and memoranda). There is only one Libro
compere extant in the Selfridge Collection. It is MS 516, one of a set of books for a
partnership in the cloth industry, called Giuliano di Giovenco and Francesco di
Giuliano [his son] de’ Medici and Company, for the years 1491-1495, with a few
memoranda up to 1499. In the corresponding ledger, MS 514, the entries after
1492 are missing. The other related books referred to in the ledger—an Entrata e

MEDICI METHODS OF BOOKKEEPING 371

Uscita (income and outgo), a Quaderno di cassa (cash book), a Libro tintori e lavoranti
(book of dyers and workmen), and a Libro tessitori (book of weavers) are all lost.

This one example may be considered as characteristic of the Medici Sales and
Purchase books of the fifteenth century. The first nineteen folios are devoted to
purchases of wool, alum, dyestuffs, etc., needed in the manufacture of woolen cloth.
Foll. 20-89 are the sales book, foll. 89-114 contain a record of all cloth sold by the cut
referring back to the sales section for each sale of a cut piece of cloth. Here is one
account for cloth sold by the cut and one of the accounts from the sales section to

Foll. 115-129 of the Libro compere are a rent book and a wage book for the
salaries of the employees in the shop. (The wages to artisans are in the Libro
tessitori and the Libro tintori e lavoranti.) The last section of the thick volume is
that of Ricordanze, memoranda containing contracts with apprentices and factors,
leases for the shop, terms of commissions to agents, etc., and invoices of shipments as
well as accounts of carriage and shipping charges.

The entries in the purchase and sales sections of this book are of the same type
as those found in the journals of the sixteenth century, except that the A used before
debit entries and the Da used before credit entries in the journals are lacking in the
Book of Purchases and Sales.

Most of the purchase and sale entries are posted to the ledger. Some cash
sales are posted to the Cash Book and a few to the Book of Income (entrata)—why
both are used is not clear. A few cash purchases are posted to the Book of Outgo
(uscita).

The section on cloth sold by the cut is not found in any of the journals, but
some journals contain a stock list of all the cloth manufactured and the itemized
accounts of its sale by whole lengths of cloth, not by cut pieces. The rent and wage
accounts found in the fourth section of the Libro compere are found mingled with all
other kinds of entries in the regular journals. A number of the journals do contain
memoranda (ricordanze) similar to those found in MS 516.

The oldest journal in the Selfridge Collection is a personal one for 1476 to 1491.
The next five are banking journals dating from 1484 to 1492. These are followed by
three for the dyeing industry, 1498-1515, and one for the cloth trade, 1503-1505.
The earliest journal for cloth-manufacturing dates from 1513. From then until
1559 there is an almost unbroken series of industrial journals. These will be studied
here with occasional references to some of the other journals for dyeing, etc.

The journals are called either giornale alone or giornale e ricordanze (journal
and memoranda) depending upon whether notes and memoranda are kept in the
rear of the journal or not. Two-thirds of the journals have in the rear memoranda
such as were described under the Libro compere, the forerunner of the journal in the
Medici account books, namely contracts with employees, shop leases, commissions
to agents, invoices and carriage charges. Some journals have examples of all of
these, others, only of a few of these types of memoranda. A third section found in
some journals—never included in the title, but sometimes listed on the title-page
when an index of the pages devoted to each of the three sections is given—is one
called tavole di panni finiti (tables of cloths sold). It is a stocklist of all the cloth
manufactured for a given partnership and contains a summary account of all the
sales made of complete lengths of cloth. A separate table is begun for each lot of
cloth as it is placed in stock. Each lot or bale has a mark or number and the indi-
vidual pieces of cloth belonging to a given lot are frequently numbered as in the
second example given here below:

None of the Medici journals follow the form of the Venetian ones described by
Paciolo. Instead of using Per for a Debit entry, the Medici journals use A, and in
place of the A which means Credit in Venetian journals, Da is used in the Florentine
ones. A for debits is used in the sense of “sold to,” “given to,” etc. Da for credits
means “purchased from,” received from,” etc. Below is an example of a Debit entry
for a sale:

In the example Andrea di Sorgo is debited on page 11 of the ledger for cloth
purchased and the Cloth account is credited on p. 12 of the ledger. The credit is not
definitely specified in this journal entry or in most of the Medici debit journal entries,
contrary to the practice described by Paciolo, in which each journal entry began with
the debit and was followed by the credit, the debit always appearing first. In the
Medici journals credits as well as debits appear alone, although the dual nature of the
transaction is expressed through the reference to two ledger pages which are given
for most journal entries. Here is an example of a credit entry:

A and Da are not the only terms used to designate Debit and Credit in the
journals. Fa debitore—(e) creditore (make debtor and creditor) is sometimes used.
instead, but not in any of the journals for woolen-cloth manufacturing. This phrase
is found in two of the dyers’ journals, MS 551 (1), 1502-1509, and MS 544 (1), 1505-
1515, and in one personal journal of 1557-1560. A second journal for personal
expenses, MS 568 (3), 1566-1569, uses Debitore and Creditore without Fa. Here is

It is to be noted that when Fa debitore—(e) creditore is used the debit always
appears first and the credit is clearly designated by name. Also the ledger pages are
given in the left-hand margin. Both these features resemble modern methods of
bookkeeping more than do the entries which use A and Da and which have the ledger-
page references in the center of the page under each entry.

When the ledger references are in the center of the page, something more than
the two figures is written before the page numbers—either a libro, or a longer expres-
sion such as a libro rosso (or whatever may be the color of the ledger referred to), a
libro segno K, a libro debitori segno C, or a still longer phrase such as posto debitore (or
creditore) a libro rosso (posted debtor or creditor to the red ledger) or posto dare (or
avere) a libro rosso (posted debit or credit to the red ledger).

The explanation for using the name of the general ledger appears when we find
page references to the special wage ledger—al quaderno di manifattori c. 18. To help
distinguish between the two ledgers, when both are referred to in the journal, only one
page reference is ever given for the wage ledger in journal entries. The journals in
which the ledger pages appear in the left-hand margins are personal ones and journals
for dyers, none of which has any corresponding wage ledgers, so that it is not neces-
sary to distinguish between two ledgers, as is necessary in the sixteenth-century
journals of the cloth-manufacturing firms.

In none of the Medici journals is the modern practice of using two effective
columns followed, one money column only being used invariably.

It will be noted in the illustrations from journals given above that several
journal entries were posted from another book, a guadernaccio or wastebook. This is
true for all of the journals for cloth-manufacturing from 1498 to 1534. Only three
wastebooks are extant. The oldest one, for 1493-1496, is called memoriale, the name
given to the wastebook, or book of primary entry in Paciolo. The other two, from
1552-1565 and 1558-1571, are called quadernacci, as are all the wastebooks referred
to in the journals.

‘The purpose and usefulness of the wastebooks found in the Selfridge Collection
are not clear, because the entries in these books are practically identical in form and
substance with those in the corresponding journals. The entries are in paragraph
form as in the journals. In the memoriale, MS 535, A and Da are used for Debit and
Credit entries, and all the postings are to the journal. In the two quadernacci,

MEDICI METHODS OF BOOKKEEPING Oe

MSS 563 and 600 (6), A and Da are used for entries which are posted to the journal,
but Fa debitore—e creditore also appears. Whenever this term is used, the entry is
posted to the general ledger and the two ledger page references are given in the left-
hand margin. It is not at all clear why certain types of entries are posted directly
from the wastebook to the ledger. Some of these entries are for fixtures, a few are
for expenses charged to real accounts, and most of them are for payments to creditors
made by transferring accounts receivable to the creditors’ accounts. In the corre-
sponding ledger entries, no reference is made to the wastebook, and, of course, none
is made to the journal in which these entries do not appear at all.

We have just described the three fundamental books of double-entry book-
keeping used by the Medici—the wastebook, the journal or the stock book, and the
ledger. We shall now turn to the special journals and ledgers, the most common of
which are the Book of Income and Outgo (entrata e uscita) and the Cash Book (quad-
erno di cassa). Frequently they are combined in one volume. The Cash Book
cannot be described because no example of it is extant. The individual cash books
are missing and the pages devoted to the Quaderno di cassa have been torn out of each
Entrata e Uscita book.

Six volumes of Entrata e Uscita are extant. Three of them originally contained
cash books (quaderno di cassa) as well as entries for Income and Outgo for the general
and the special wage ledgers, MS 567 (12), 1534-1540, MS 558 (3), 1541-1549, and
MS 568 (6), 1556-1559. Two of the others, MS 555 (3), 1530-1524, and MS 558 (6),
1536-1538, are combinations of Income and Outgo in the first part and of a ledger in
the second part, to which the entries under Income, etc., are posted. The remaining
book, MS 600 (3), 1525-1531, the oldest one in the group, is a book of Income and
Outgo for the wage ledger only.

1 Medici MS 563, fol. 147.
? Ivid., fol. 61%.

MEDICI METHODS OF BOOKKEEPING

The three Entrata e Uscita first mentioned had originally five sections:

(1) Entrata del libro grande (income of the general ledger)

(2) Uscita del libro grande (outgo of the general ledger)

(3) Entrata del quaderno di manifattori (income of the wage ledger)

(4) Uscita del quaderno di manifattori (outgo of the wage ledger)

(5) Quaderno di cassa (cash book).
All the cash which came into the business is entered in section one of the special
journal and each entry is posted to the general ledger. All the money paid out
for purchases and to the partners for their drawings is listed in section two and
posted to the general ledger. Here are also found entries for money transferred from
the Cash account in the main ledger to the Cash account in the wage ledger out of
which wages were paid. All the money and services in terms of money received from
workmen for purchases of cloth, etc., and from the shop expense account (spese di
bottega) are found in the third section, and are posted to the wage ledger. In the
fourth, appear all entries for money paid out in wages, commissions, etc., the items
being posted to the wage ledger. The last section, the so-called Cash Book, is missing
from these books. It may have contained summaries of all the entries in the other
sections. It is not referred to very frequently in the sixteenth-century ledgers
which had Cash accounts within the ledgers. It was apparently more important
in the fifteenth century, when there were no Cash accounts in the ledgers.

The only trial balances found in any of the Medici account books are in the
Books of Income and Outgo, in which the total income and expenditures are usually
balanced annually. Sometimes it is done at the end of a few months because of a
change of cashier. Sometimes there is an interval of two years or more between trial
balances. In the earliest of these books, MS 600 (3), trial balances were made on
6 February 1525 [0.s.], 28 March1526—because of a change of cashier, 18 February
1526 [o.s.], 28 June 1527—again because of a change of cashier, 31 May 1529, and 19
January 1531 [o.s.]. The form of the trial balance is very simple. The total of the
expenditures for the year (or other period of time), brought forward from the Uscita
section, is deducted from the total income and the result in each balanceis0 0 0.

Mention has already been made of the inclusion in each set of books for indus-
trial accounting in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries of one or more special journals
containing memoranda concerning raw materials and cloth given out to workmen
and the wages due them for work completed. Such memoranda books are found
also among the Datini account books of the fourteenth century. In the sixteenth
century there were usually three such journals: (1) Libro filatori (book of spinners),
(2) Libro tessitori (book of weavers), and (3) Libro tintori e lavoranti (book of dyers
and workmen). Besides the special wage journals, a special wage ledger appeared
in the sixteenth century for the first time. Most of the memoranda of wages were
posted from the special journals into the wage ledger and not into the general ledger.
However, the accounts with Janini and stamaiuoli, the wool-factors in charge of
spinning, with dyers, fullers, shearmen, and stretchers, were posted to the main ledger.
Why this was done is not clear. Of these special industrial journals, only four are
extant: two for spinners, one for weavers, and one for dyers and other workmen.

In the special journals for the spinning of wool, MS 567 (2), 1556-1557, and
MS 568 (2), 1552-1556, are the accounts with the stamaiuoli, who took combed wool
and had it spun into yarn, and with the Janini, who did the same for the carded wool.
For excerpts from one of these books see Appendix VIII. The accounts with the
stamaiuoli are always on the left-hand pages and those with the Janini, on the right-
hand. The summary of the amounts owed the stamaiuoli and the lanini are posted
directly to the general ledger, not to the wage ledger.

In the special journal for warping and weaving (libro tessitori), MS 560 (5),
1547-1552, accounts were kept with the warpers and the weavers. In this book the
accounts are arranged under the heading for a given lot of cloth, a heading which
runs across two pages facing each other. On the left-hand page is recorded the
amounts of worsted yarn given out to the warpers who prepared the warp for each
piece of cloth. On the right-hand page there is recorded the weight of the warp and
of the weft yarn given to each weaver for one piece of cloth. For examples from
these pages see Appendix IX. In the rear of the book are kept the accounts with the
individual warpers and weavers that are posted to the wage ledger.

Tn the special journal for steps in the woolen industry, other than spinning,
warping, and weaving, entitled Libro tintori e lavoranti (book of dyers and workmen)
MS 567 (7), 1556, the following table of contents is found on the title-page:

the accounts with Batista di Pasquino, the capodieci, in charge of the process of

The last account book to be introduced into the sets of industrial books used by
the Medici was the Quaderno di manifattori (ledger of workmen), in which most of the

1 Medici MS 567 (7), fol. 30°.

MEDICI METHODS OF BOOKKEEPING 385

accounts with workmen, industrial factors, and apprentices were kept. Four of the
account books are extant. The earliest one is for 1520-1521 and the latest for 1556-
1559. No reference to a wage ledger earlier than 1520 has been found in any of the
other account books. The ledgers of workmen contain a number of impersonal ac-
counts—a Cash account, a general expense account (spese fatte per questa ragione di
nostro conto), a brokerage account, a Profit and Loss account, a Cost of Manufactur-
ing account, and an account for the General Ledger which is the controlling account
for all the money paid out through the wage ledger. Most of the real accounts, for
wool, cloth, etc., appear in the general ledger, but some of the wage ledgers have
accounts for oil which was used in preparing the wool for combing and carding.

Under the expense account (spese fatte per questa ragione di nostro conto) there
are debits for the set of account books, for charcoal and fire, for wool-combs, for
teasels used in napping cloth, and there are many entries for undefined expenses, all
of which are posted from the Book of Outgo or expenditures. The expense account
is credited with the total amount paid out, which is debited to Cost of Manufacture.
The latter account is debited with all the sums paid out in wages, commissions, and
salaries. It was balanced by crediting the account for the total amount paid out
and by debiting the General Ledger account.
