There are three groups of business account books other than those for industrial
partnerships in the manufacture and sale of woolen cloth. One group deals with the
cloth trade as distinct from the manufacturing of cloth. Another group concerns
two Medici firms of dyers of cloth. The third group is a series of books for partner-
ships in banking and the sale of articles of luxury. The numerous estate account
books and the few personal expense account books will not be discussed here.

The typical set of books for the cloth trade consisted of a journal, a ledger, a
letter book (copialettere), a copybook of invoices (copia di legaggi), which was some-
times bound with the letter book, and a copybook of notes and memoranda of carriage
and shipping charges (libro di ricordanze), which was sometimes combined with the
journal, in which case the combined volume was called giornale e ricordanze. In only
two ledgers for the cloth trade is any mention made of a book of Income and Outgo
(entrata e uscita). All the books of this group fall within a period of thirty years,
from 1495 to 1525, and they deal principally with the exporting of cloth to the Levant
and the importing of silk, spices, etc., in exchange.

The ledgers for the cloth trade have more real accounts than do the industrial

1 Medici MS 507 (11), fol. 427.

MEDICI METHODS OF BOOKKEEPING 387

ones. For every shipment of cloth, every amount of silk or of spices received, a
separate account is opened. Many of the accounts are for goods sold on commission,
since sometimes the Medici paid commissions to agents and sometimes they them-
selves acted as agents and received commissions on the goods they sold. All the
separate ventures are closed into Profit and Loss and all the commissions paid or
received are posted to that account. The principal impersonal accounts, besides the
Profit and Loss one, were a Cash account, an Expense account for cloth (spese di
panni), and Insurance accounts, each insurance agreement being treated as a sepa-
rate venture. The books were probably closed through the Profit and Loss account,
but we cannot be certain because the last pages are missing from all the trade ledgers.

The letter books contain correspondence with agents in Ancona (the seaport
from which Florentine cloth was shipped to the East), in Ragusa, in Pera, Brusa,
etc. The invoices are copies of those sent with the shipments of goods from Florence,
and the accounts of carriage charges are copies of such accounts sent in by agents
showing all of the expenses involved in transporting cloth from Florence to the
Levant or in shipping Levantine products to Florence.

The account books used by the Medici dyers between 1498 and 1515 were a
wastebook, a journal, a ledger, a book of Income and Outgo—all of which were used
by some of the firms of cloth-manufacturers as has been shown, and two unfamiliar
books. One was a book of cloth-manufacturers (libro lanaiuoli) containing memo-
randa of cloth received for dyeing, the dates cloth was returned, and the amounts
due from the manufacturers, which corresponded to the book of dyers kept by the
woolen-cloth manufacturers. The other was called Libro aluminati or Libro degli
aluminati. It had something to do with alum, but the references to the book in
the ledgers do not make clear its purpose, and no example of such a book is extant in
the Selfridge Collection. Alum was the principal mordant used in the dyeing of
cloth. This book may have contained records of the cloths bathed in alum, the
amount of alum used for a given lot of cloth, and the charges made for this step in the
dyeing process.

The simplest set of books is that used by the Medici in banking between 1482
and 1494. There were only four books—a journal, a ledger, a book of Income and
Outgo and Cash book combined, and a book of memoranda (ricordanze) which was
sometimes combined with the journal. The memorandum book contained records
of all loans made, with the terms, etc. They were frequently signed by the bor-
rowers. The ledger contained very few impersonal accounts—one was called “Bank
Expenses,” others were for jewels, belts, and other articles of luxury handled by the
bankers. Only one of the three extant bank ledgers has a Profit and Loss account.
None of the three books is complete. Postings were made from the journal to
Income, Outgo, or the Cash book, and from these divisions of the special journal to
the ledger.

Certain details—pagination, cancellation of accounts, use of numerals, etc.,
have been left until the end for treatment. There are two predominating sizes
among the Medici books—a large folio volume with pages measuring 11} inches by
163 inches and a small folio volume with pages measuring 83 inches or 9 inches by
11 inches to 13 inches. The large volumes are general ledgers and special journals

388 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

for workmen (libri filatori, tessitori, tintori e lavoranti). The smaller volumes are
wastebooks, journals, stock books, letter books, books of Income and Outgo, a few of
the general ledgers, and all the special ledgers. There is a very small group of
miscellaneous account books with pages 6 inches by 83 inches. There is another
small group of long, narrow books called quadernucci, a pejorative of quaderno. They
are about 4 inches wide and vary in length from 11} inches to 123 inches. The
quadernucci are usually personal or estate account books.

With very few exceptions the three groups of smaller volumes are bound in
parchment, usually reinforced by strips of leather. The large volumes are either
bound in parchment or in leather—some plain, some beautifully tooled. The parch-
ment cover is the usual one in the fifteenth century, the leather one is used frequently
in the sixteenth century. The covers of all the large ledgers and of many of the
smaller books were made to overlap, and there is, or was originally, a leather strap
with a buckle encircling the center of each volume. On the front of the parchment
covers a brief title of the bookis usually written across the top and below it is the sign
or mark of the company and one letter of the alphabet used to designate all the books
belonging to a given partnership. Inside the outer cover of stiff parchment or leather
there is usually, in all sizes of books, an inner cover or pair of fly-leaves of parchment
or vellum. In the sixteenth-century books these fly-leaves are frequently formed
from sheets of manuscripts—chiefly biblical and juridical works—with rubricated
initials and a few illuminations.

Next to the fly-leaf is the title-page. Running across the top is the year date in
Roman numerals, always preceded by the sign of the Cross, and sometimes by the

letters IHS as well. Below the date is an invocation to the Omnipotent God, to the
Virgin Mary, and to many of the saints, calling upon them all to grant the merchants
good profit with the salvation of their souls and bodies:

+ mccccxxxi!

Al nome sia del omnipotente Iddio e della sua santisima madre madona santa Maria virgine
e del beato messer santo Giovanni batista e del beato messer santo Piero e del beato messer
santo Pacholo apostoli e del beato messer santo Antonio e del beato messer santo Giuliano e
di tutta la cielestralle chorte di paradiso che per loro grazia e miserichordia ci chonciedano
ghuadangnio e chon salvamento del animo e del chorpo. Amen.

The invocation is followed by the name of the individual, the partners or the
partnership, and the full title of the book. The date when the book is opened is
sometimes added:

Questo libro è di Giovencho d’Antonio de’ Medici e di Giovencho di Giuliano de’ Medici e
chonpangni lanaiuoli nel chonvento di Samartino di Firenze e chiamasi libro debitori e
creditori segno A.”

This book belongs to Giovenco d’Antonio de’ Medici and Giovenco di Giuliano de’ Medici
and companions, woolen-cloth manufacturers, in the District of San Martino in Florence,
and it is called Book of Debtors and Creditors marked A.

An index to the sections of the book is sometimes given on the title-pages of
journals, stock books, books of Income and Outgo, and books of Dyers and Workmen.
Here is an example from a journal:

Da c.1ac. 79 giornale? From p. 1 to p. 79 journal
Dac. 80 a c. 149 tavola di panni finiti From p. 80 to p. 149 table of cloths sold
Da c. 150 a resto richordanze From p. 150 to the end—memoranda

The paper used in all of the account books is of an excellent, durable quality
which has remained white and has retained the ink very well.

The pagination is by folio rather than by page. The folios are numbered on the
recto with Roman or Arabic numerals—the ledgers usually have Roman, the smaller
books either type of numeral. In a number of the ledgers and in a few of the other
books the page opposite the numbered folio sheet, i.e., the verso of the preceding folio,
has an Arabic numeral corresponding to the number on the recto of the opposite
folio. For example, in a ledger the Debit pages would have Arabic numerals corre-
sponding to the Roman numerals on the opposite Credit pages. Arabic 1 would be
on the rear of the title-page opposite folio 1", which would have a Roman I. When
both Arabic and Roman numerals are used in a book it is clear that a reference to
page 3 (carta 3) means either fol. 3" or the opposite page, fol. 2". But when only one
set of numerals is used, i.e., when only the recto of each folio is numbered, a reference
to p. 3 may mean either fol. 3", 3”, or 2%, except in the case of double-entry ledgers,
when the corresponding debit and credit pages would always be referred to. Usually
only one practice is followed in one account book; in one book, p. 3 may refer to foll.
3" and 3Y, in another book it may refer to foll. 3" and 2%. In someof the earlier books,
however, for example, M.S 496, there is a confusion of the two systems within one
book. On fol. 5" in this book there is a reference to an account on p. 57 which refers
to one on fol. 56", while another reference to the same page refers to an account found
on fol. 57".

The date of the year in the account books is always given at the top of each
page in the center. It is always in Roman numerals, usually preceded by the sign of
the Cross. In the entries dates are usually in Arabic numerals.

The pages of the accounts are ruled in pencil with a left-hand margin and one or
more effective or money columns on the right side of each page. Lines drawn hori-
zontally across the pages to separate accounts are in ink. Such lines never extend
out into the left-hand margin.

In the narrative column money figures are found in Roman or Arabic numerals.
The oldest account book, MS 492, 1406-18, uses Arabic numbers in this column.
Most of the ledgers use Roman numerals in the narrative part.

1 Medici MS 560 (4), title-page.
2 Loc. cit.

390 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

In the effective columns of all the business and estate account books Roman
numerals are used until 1439, when Giovenco di Giovenco de’ Medici uses Arabic
numbers in his estate ledger, MS 497. From then on Roman numerals are used in
all the business ledgers until that of 1482, MS 542 (1). For another decade, until
1494, they continue to be used in the business ledgers of one Medici—Giuliano di
Giovenco—but not in the ledgers of the same period kept by other Medici merchants.
Arabic numerals appear even in the money columns of the banking ledgers between
1484 and 1494. From 1494 on, only Arabic numerals are used in the effective
columns of all the ledgers. All the other kinds of account books use Arabic numerals
after 1439.

When additions of the money columns are made, the figures for the totals are
always placed in the narrative column just to the left of the money columns and the
figures are always, even in the earliest books, in Arabic numerals.

The monetary units used in the effective columns are either lire, soldi, and
denari, or florins, soldi, and denari. Sometimes both are used in one account and
four columns appear, thus: f.1.s.d. In one ledger, MS 536 (4), 1503, there are two
parallel columns for florins and lire, each with space for soldi and denari, thus:
f. s. d. 1. s. d. Because there were several kinds of florin used in Florence at any
one time—gold florins and florins which were money of account for silver—the
effective columns usually have an abbreviation for the kind of florin used in a given
set of accounts. This abbreviation is written in at the top of the column on each
page and sometimes at the beginning of each account. Some of the abbreviations
are; Li meaning fiorini larghi, Gi meaning fiorini larghi di grossi, di °or a oro meaning
fiorini larghi d’oro in oro.

Cancellation of accounts that have been posted to another book (i.e., entries in
wastebooks and in all kinds of journals, or ledger accounts which have been balanced)
is usually done by means of diagonal strokes of the pen running across a page or part
of a page. In the wastebooks and journals each entry has a diagonal stroke across
its narrative portion. Frequently a stroke across the full length of the page is added
to show that the entire page has been posted.

In the ledgers there are usually one or more parallel diagonal strokes through
each account and in addition there are short strokes through the capital letter of each
entry—the letter always being written in the left-hand margin, where it stands out
from the body of the narrative—or through the lira or florin sign of each sum entered
in the money column. These short strokes are the ticks placed before or after each
entry in the ledger when that book is checked with the journal to see that all the
journal entries have been posted twice to the ledger. The general journals do not
appear to have their corresponding checks before each entry, but the Books of
Income and Outgo have a system of cancellation which resembles closely that
described by Paciolo in his chapter on checking the journal with the ledger when
balancing the books. He suggests using one or two ticks or dots before each entry
in the journal or above and below the money sign in the effective column. When two
dots.or checks are used one is for the debit entry in the ledger and the second one is
for the credit entry there. All the Income entries in the Medici Libri entrata e uscita
begin with the word Da (from). In all but one book each D has a check in front of it

MEDICI METHODS OF BOOKKEEPING 391

or through it, thus: 2Da, Ba. In MS 600 (3), 1525-1531, there are two marks, the

check and a diagonal stroke, thus: Ja. In the Outgo sections, A (to) is the intro-
ductory word for each entry. It is always written with a large closed loop, thus:
o-. Ineach loop a dot is placed to show the entry has been checked with the ledger.
In one special journal, MS 568 (6), 1556-1559, there are two dots in each loop, cy,
and in MS 600 (3) there is one dot and one stroke through each loop, gt.

In only one of the ledgers have dots been found. This is a banking ledger, MS
532, 1488-1489. The dots appear in the left-hand margin before each capital letter
at the beginning of each entry. There are also diagonal strokes through each account
and through each page.

These methods of cancellation show that the Medici were careful in comparing
their books, even though they did not balance them as frequently as is done today.

APPENDIX III

CREDIT TRANSACTIONS IN THE MEDICI ACCOUNTS OF THE
FIFTEENTH AND SIXTEENTH CENTURIES

In the Middle Ages the three Florentine gilds, namely, the Arte di Calimala,
Arte di Seta, and Arte di Lana, whose members did a large export business, attempted
to regulate credit terms for the protection of their members. In the Calimala
statutes of the fourteenth century, terms for credit were usually limited to 23 or 33
months with one week’s grace. During the fifteenth century the time limits were
extended to 6 and 8 months with two months’ grace.

According to the earliest statutes of the Wool Gild, those of 1317 and 1330,
credit was limited to 23 months, but by 1333 it was extended to a maximum of 4
months for the sale of cloth, and a minimum of 5 months for the purchase of wool,
dyestuffs, and other raw materials used in the woolen cloth industry. In other
words, a wool merchant, who was purchasing materials on time, was not supposed to
accept terms of less than 5 months from the seller. In introducing a maximum credit
term for sales, which was less than the minimum term for purchases, the gild was
apparently protecting the small merchant who could not afford to give long credit
but who would be helped by receiving long credit.

In the Wool Gild statutes of the fifteenth century the time limit for both pur-
chases and sales was increased to 8 months and then to one year. Revisions and
additions to these statutes were made up to the year 1589. Doren, whose work on
the Florentine woolen industry is the principal source for the information given above,
does not mention any credit regulations for the sixteenth century. Without an
examination of the manuscript sources in the Florentine archives, it is impossible to
state whether the sixteenth-century provisions did or did not alter or abolish the
earlier time limits for credit transactions in the woolen cloth industry.

The Calimala and Silk Gilds made definite regulations concerning discount and
indemnity for late payments, usually prescribing two denari per lira per month, a
rate of 10% per year, both for payments made before the term and for delayed
payments. The Wool Gild, however, never included in its statutes any definite
regulations regarding discount or interest on credit transactions.

Sapori, in his study of the books of Francesco Del Bene, a fourteenth-century
Calimala merchant (Una Compagnia di Calimala ai primi del Trecento), found that
the provisions of the Calimala statutes regarding credit terms were observed. An
examination of the fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Medici account books in the
Selfridge Collection, in particular those dealing with the woolen industry, has
revealed that the statutory time limits for credit were not strictly observed during
the fifteenth century. Terms of 15 and 18 months have been found as early as 1442
(MS 498, foll. 7%, 14"), when the limit was supposed to be one year. These examples,
however, are not numerous; most of the credit terms listed in the fifteenth-century

392

CREDIT TRANSACTIONS 393

account books are for less than one year. In the books of the Medici of the sixteenth
century terms for sales from 14 to 20 months are not uncommon, but in the vast
majority of cases the terms are for one year or less—commonly 4 to 8 months.

These account books also show that there was no uniform practice as regards
discount and interest. Clear cases of discount or interest for overdue payments are
rarely found, possibly because they were deliberately kept out of the journals and
ledgers. Furthermore, the sale price of cloth for cash was frequently as high as the
price for credit, especially in the fifteenth century. This situation was in accord
with the teaching of the Church, which denounced any increase in the price of goods
sold for credit. In the sixteenth century the price of cloth was often raised approxi-
mately one lira for each 6 months of credit; for example, a cloth selling for 30 lire, 15
soldi per canna for cash was sold for 31 lire on terms of 4 and 5 months and for 32 lire,
10 soldi for terms of one year and also of 18 months. The sales of two lots of black
accordellata cloth found in a journal of 1548, M.S 560 (4), may be tabulated as follows:

About one-half of the wholesale cloth sales, exclusive of those sales made in
exchange for other goods, were for credit, and the other half for cash. Most of the
retail sales, i.e., cuts of cloth or full-length pieces sold to individuals to be used for
clothing and not to be resold, were for cash. But it was not exceptional to make
retail sales for credit, usually giving 4, 5, or 8 months’ time. The ledgers show that
in cash sales payments were frequently made within one week of the date of purchase,
and with very few exceptions, not later than one month from that date. One may
conclude that in sales made for cash, not immediate payment, but payment within
one month of the sales-entry, was understood.

Among the Medici account books the best sources for a study of credit trans-
actions in the woolen cloth industry and trade are the journals, in which the terms
for sales and purchases are given in much greater detail than in the ledgers. These
journals are all of the sixteenth century. There are nine in the Selfridge Collection
dealing with the woolen industry from 1503 to 1571. (A few fifteenth-century
journals are extant, but they deal with banking and with a Medici firm of dyers, not
with the Medici as wool-merchants.) The ledgers, of which there are numerous
examples, for the fifteenth as well as the sixteenth centuries, occasionally repeat the
credit terms stated in full in the journals, but frequently the terms are omitted, so
that the only clue as to whether a transaction was for cash or credit is the date or
dates of payment. Therefore most of the statements made below regarding length
of terms, payments overdue, etc., are based on sixteenth-century material. The
journals give the credit terms, and the corresponding ledgers show when the pay-
ments were made.

The first conclusion one draws from a comparison of journals and ledgers is
that, while credit terms were clearly and exactly stated and drawn up, they were
seldom observed in the making of payments, so seldom, that, with the exception of
one group of credit terms, payments made according to the terms agreed upon are
hard to find in the ledgers. The situation is perhaps comparable to that in modern
business houses in which good customers are not pressed to meet the terms upon
which they have purchased goods. No instances of interest charges on overdue
payments have been found in the account books but we cannot conclude from this
absence that they were never made, as the tendency would be to conceal such charges
and not to record them openly in the ledgers. A very few examples of discount for
full or partial payments made several months before the termination of the credit
terms have been found (see Appendix IV).

CREDIT TRANSACTIONS 399

The terms for purchases of raw materials (wool, dyestuffs, oil, etc.), of which
comparatively few were made by the Medici on a credit basis, range from one month
to 16 months, the most popular terms being one year, payable on the date due (per
tempo dell’anno pagati il di del tempo), and 5 or 6 months, either payable on the date
due or payable during the 2 months following the expiration of the term, one-half of
the debt being due each month (per tempo di mesi 5 e di poi ogni mese la metà).

For sales of cloth the terms range from one month to 20 months. More than
half of all the terms examined are for less than one year—one month to 11 months—
although the term of one year is more frequently found than that for any other
single period of time in almost all the Medici journals and ledgers. The popularity
of credit for one year, even in the fifteenth century is attested by the fact that in
some of the ledgers of that century the expression per lo termine (on the [usual] terms),
is used to mean terms for one year. This expression is never found in the sixteenth-
century account books, where tempo is always used in place of termine and is always
followed by a definite length of time (per tempo dell’anno, per tempo di mesi 18, etc.).

The terms used in the journals kept between 1503 and 1571! may be arranged in
several groups according to certain key phrases used in stating the terms, such as iI
dì del tempo, e di poi ogni mese ... , in due paghe, etc. The first phrase, il di del
tempo (on the date due) is the most common one. It occurs in the following terms:

perenne ipa, il dì del tempo
per tempo di mesi 1-16, 18, 20 il dì del tempo —time—1-16, 18 or 20 months on the date due

time—one year on the date due

Sometimes the phrase tutto în una partita (allin one sum) is added (per tempo dell’anno
il dì del tempo tutto in una partita), and sometimes it is used in place of il dì del tempo
(per tempo di mesi sei tutto in una partita). This is the only group of credit terms for
which the dates of payment found in the ledgers show any definite relation to the
actual terms of the sales. An examination of numerous sixteenth-century ledgers
reveals the fact that almost one-half of the sales and purchases made with terms
up to and including 5 months were paid for within a period of 2 weeks following the
expiration of the time, and that approximately one-half of the sales made with terms
of 6 months to one year or more were paid for within one month of the date of expira-
tion of the term. It would appear, therefore, that during the sixteenth century
there was a period of 2 weeks’ grace for credit terms of one month to 5 months, and
of one month’s grace for credit terms of 6 months or more. If we grant that these
two periods of grace were allowed, then about one-half of the sales and purchases
made on terms of one month’s to 20 months’ time, payable on the date due, were paid
on time. The payments were sometimes made in one sum, sometimes in install-
ments. When the phrase tutto in una partita is present, the payment is usually in
one sum, but not always.

The second group of terms centers about the phrase di poi ogni mese ... (and
then each month ... ):

(3), 1525-1534; 554 (4), 1530-1534; 554 (1), 1534-1541; 560 (4), 1547-1553; 600 (6), 1558-1571.

per tempo dell’anno e di poi ogni mese la _ time—one year and then one-half or 3, etc.,
metà, 3, 3, 3,3 to be paid each succeeding month.
per tempo di mesi — e di poi ogni mese la time—so many months, and then }, etc.,
metà, 3, 4, 3,3 of the amount to be paid each succeeding
month after the date due.

Ogni mese is sometimes omitted, so that the phrase reads e di poi } (after the date due
[each month]). Of the terms, one-half, one-third, etc., one-half is most frequently
found, and secondly, one-fourth. According to this group of terms, equal payments
were to be made during the 2 to 6 months after the expiration of the time, e.g., if a
man bought cloth on terms of one year and then each month one-fifth, he would
presumably pay one-fifth of the total amount due during each of the first 5 months
following the expiration of the term of one year, that is during the thirteenth to
seventeenth months. The record of payments made in the ledgers show that these
terms were rarely adhered to. Whether the payments were to be 2 or 6 in number,
the correct number of payments was rarely made and very seldom during the speci-
fied months, late payments being very common. Furthermore, payments were
seldom made in equal installments, even when only 2 payments were called for and
made. Whether the extreme irregularity shown in the making of payments, when
the credit terms were of this rather complicated type, may be regarded as evidence
that these credit terms concealed some form of usurious practice is a question that
may be raiséd at this point, but that cannot be solved by the source material at hand.

The third phrase, pagati in due paghe (paid in two payments) is far less common
than either of the two discussed above:

time—one year, or so many months, paid
in 2 payments

per tempo dell’anno

dici a pagati in 2 paghe

No example of this phrase being used in connection with a term of less than six
months has been found. The payments were always made after the termination of
the specified time, and not necessarily in two payments, 3 and 4 (never more) pay-
ments being as frequently found in the ledgers as 2 payments. The installments
were rarely equal in amount, and the time when they were paid varied greatly (from
a month toa year anda half after the term).

Less frequently found than the first three groups are terms of so many florins
per week, per fortnight, or per month:

a darne f. — il mese to give of the amount f. — each month

The first fair was held in January, the second in April, the third in August, and
the fourth in November. Each fair lasted fifteen days. Why the Lyons fairs were
sometimes used in fixing the terms for credit transactions is not clear. A Spaniard, a
Lucchese, and other Italians whose names do not appear to be Florentine, but who
are not specifically designated as non-Florentines, are those to whom credit is given
in connection with the Lyons fairs. The fairs are usually associated with exchange
transactions, but only Florentine money is mentioned in the entries in the account
books; however, payment in other coinage may have been involved, or possibly some
form of surreptitious usury.

Terms of part cash and part credit are not very common, but do appear a few
times in most of the journals:

a darcene di presente f.100 il resto tempo to give us 100 florins today, the balance,
mesi 4 prossimi il di del tempo® time—4 months on the date due.

a darci alla mano f.300 e del resto tempo to give into our hands f.300 and the balance,
mesi 37 time—3 months.

only once or twice in an entire journal. For example, instead of the more usual

monta di detto tempo di mesi otto in una partita et la metà tempo di 14 mesi in due
paghe for half of the amount due terms of 8 months in one payment, and for the

The Medici sold cloth to Piero Ispina and Co., Silk Merchants. After the sale
was completed, a member of the Medici firm went to the shop of the silk merchants and
examined their books, or one of their books, to see that the purchase of cloth on credit
was properly entered in the Ispina books as a debt due the Medici, their creditors for
the cloth purchased. The Medici partner, or factor, or bookkeeper, or cashier, upon
his return had the bookkeeper enter in the ledger on the debit side of the Ispina
account the statement that the proper credit entry had been found in the Ispina
Memorandum or Daybook marked B on page 96.

Sometimes the Medici bookkeeper added the date when the debtor’s book was
examined. This date is usually within a week or so of the sale. For example, after
an entry for cloth sold 29 April 1483 appears the statement that the purchase was
seen recorded in the debtor’s book on 5 May (Veduti iscritti in dì 5 di magio a libro
loro richordanze segnato B c. 35).4

The wording of this type of statement is sometimes varied in the ledgers as
follows:

Veduto ciene creditori a libro loro, etc. Seen ourselves as creditors for that amount
in their book, etc.

Siamo creditori a libro loro, etc. We are creditors in their book, etc.

Ano ciene creditori a libro loro, etc. They have us as creditors for the amount in
in their book, etc.

This practice is followed in most of the Medici ledgers of the fifteenth century,
but there are no examples of it in the sixteenth-century ledgers. For the latter
century we must turn to the journals, where, in the rear, in a special section called
Ricordanze (records, memoranda), are grouped together all the statements of the
examination of debtors’ books by members or employees of the Medici firm. (Other
material is included in the Ricordanze, such as copies of bills of exchange, bills of
lading, invoices, etc.) The form of the verifying statement—if we may call it that
—found in the sixteenth-century journals is longer than that found in the fifteenth-
century ledgers, because of the fact that the journal statements are detached from
the records of the sales to which they relate, instead of being attached to the related
entries as they are in the ledgers.

Three examples of the Ricordanze are given below. It will be noted that there
is less variation in phrasing in the journal records than was found in the ledger
records.

No explanation has been found for this interesting practice of examining records
of accounts of credit sales in the purchasers’ books and recording the fact in the

1 MS 552, fol. 1517.
2 MS 554 (4), fol. 151”.
3 Loc. cit.

404 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

sellers’ books. Neither the gild nor municipal statutes mention it. It was not done
only in the case of a certain type of credit or a certain class of customer. Most of
the customers of the Medici whose books were examined were Florentine merchants,
wool merchants, silk merchants, retail dealers, gold-beaters, etc. A very few, such
as the merchant in Ragusa whose books were examined by a traveling agent of the
Medici in Ragusa, were merchants residing outside of Florence.

For only a small percentage—less than ‘one-fourth—of the sales of cloth
recorded in the sixteenth-century journals was this type of verification made, partly
because many sales were made to non-Florentine merchants whose books could not
be easily examined. The verifications are more numerous in the ledgers of the
fifteenth century, being made for about one-third of the sales in some ledgers, and
almost one-half in others.

One of the very puzzling factors in connection with this practice is the fact that
almost every credit transaction which was examined in the debtor’s book was also
recorded in a broker’s book. The broker’s record was sufficient proof of the exist-
ence of a debt. The verifications described above appear to be unnecessary duplica-
tions of evidence, yet if the missing clue could only be found this unusual practice
would doubtless prove to have been a very sound one.

APPENDIX IV
DISCOUNT IN THE MEDICI ACCOUNTS

The instances in which discount (sconto) is mentioned in the Medici account
books are few and occur in records of the sixteenth century only, none being found
in fifteenth-century journals or ledgers.

There were two types of discount as used in this period. The first was the dis-
count on credit sales, when payment was made before the end of the credit term and
was customarily 8% although sometimes 9% was given. The second kind of dis-
count was more unusual. The Medici, and other cloth-manufacturers, occasionally
sold cloth to their factors, their weavers, etc., and to firms of wool-washers, dyers,
etc., in exchange for services. That is to say, the price of the cloth would be
deducted from the wages of employees or from the accounts of work done by dyers,
etc., for the Medici. In such sales, the purchaser was usually given a certain number
of months in which to render services equivalent to the price of the cloth. At the end
of the term, he was to pay the balance still owing, in cash, either immediately or
within a given period. The second term for the cash period was sometimes as long
as the first for the payment in labor services. When several months’ time was
granted for the balance due in cash, a discount was allowed for the prompt payment
of the balance. This discount might be as high as 333%, as in the example quoted
below, although cloth sold for payment in the form of services was not usually sold at
a higher price than cloth sold for cash or for the regular credit terms with their dis-
count of 8 or 9%.

The following citation is from a ledger belonging to a Medici partnership of
dyers. It shows that the company of dyers had purchased cloth in exchange for
services, and that if there were a cash balance due at the end of 8 months, a discount
of } would be allowed for a prompt cash payment.

APPENDIX V

RITENZIONE IN THE MEDICI ACCOUNTS

In most of the Medici journals and ledgers belonging to the period from 1513 to
1541 there is found a practice of deducting the sum of two denari or more per sealed
gold florin (fiorino di suggello) from the selling or purchasing price of wool, cloth,
etc., whether the transaction involved cash or credit. When the Medici bought
wool, etc., they deducted two or more denari per sealed florin from the purchasing
price, usually quoted in terms of large gold florins (fiorini largo d’oro in oro), which
were 39% higher than the sealed florins. When they sold cloth, etc., they deducted
the two or more denari per sealed florin from the selling price. ‘The amount deducted
was usually two denari; but it varied from one denaro to as high as six denari per
sealed florin. This reduction of several denari per sealed florin—regardless of the
kind of gold florin used in the actual payment for the purchase—was called ritenzione
(or retenzione) and, occasionally, ditenzione (or detenzione).

Its purpose is not known. It was not a cash discount, since it was deducted
from credit transactions as well as cash ones. Nor was it a broker’s fee, because it
was deducted from transactions made without as well as those made through brokers.
There is no account in any of the ledgers to show that the ritenzione was a form of
sales tax levied by the Wool Gild or the City of Florence, a tax, that is, such as that
levied in the fifteenth century by the Silk Gild, the Arte di Por Santa Maria, on the
silk manufacturers who were required by statute to retain two denari per gold florin
from the wages they paid to weavers and other workmen, the money being turned
over to the gild. A similar fee, with the same name, was deducted from the salaries
of some of the state employees and officials in Florence. But the statutes of the
Wool Gild, the Arte della Lana, contain no provision for the collection of such a tax.

No mention of the ritenzione is found in two of the journals of the period 1513-
1541, one for 1518-1522, and another for 1521-1529. Furthermore it was not
deducted from every sale or purchase recorded in those journals in which it does
occur, although they do contain many examples. A comparison in the same journals
of the transactions from which the deduction of the several denari per sealed florin is
made with those from which it is not made reveals no clue to its purpose. Nor has
any explanation been found for the appearance of this practice during the particular
period of approximately twenty-five years, 1513-1541, which is the only time that it
appears in any of the Medici documents.

A few examples of typical journal and ledger entries illustrating the practice
are given here. In-the first one the rate of the ritenzione was over six denari per
sealed florin; in the second, the more usual one of two denari; in the third, less than
two denari per sealed florin. It is hoped that these illustrations may enable some
scholar acquainted with the documents of the period to explain the purpose of the
ritenzione as found in these Medici account books.

APPENDIX VI
WOOL-WASHERS IN FLORENCE

Wool-washers in mediaeval Florence were independent masters who with the
aid of apprentices or employees washed the wool which they received from industrial
entrepreneurs. The washing took place in the Arno River or in the canal (Ja Gora),
which may have been the canal leading to the mills located at the St. Nicholas Gate
(Porto San Niccolò) on the left bank of the Arno.

In one of the Medici account books, MS 567 (7), entitled “Book of Dyers and
Workmen” (Libro tintori e lavoranti)—a special journal in which were kept accounts
with wool-workers (except spinners and weavers, for whom there were separate
journals), cloth-finishers, and dyers—there are two folio pages of accounts with a
firm of wool-washers, “Francesco di Giovanni di Giunta and Co., Wool-Washers at
the Canal” (Lavatori alla Gora). On the first page, are itemized six lots of wool given
out to be washed during 1556 and 1557 by Francesco di Giuliano di Raffaello de’
Medici and Co. On the second page are listed the sums of money due Giunta and
Co. for the washing of the wool and for the alum which they supplied and used in
washing. This account is posted from the special journal to a special ledger for
wages and manufacturing costs (Quaderno di manifattori; see Appendix II).

The first lot of wool recorded was given to the washers on 2 May 1556. There
were twelve sacks of Spanish wool with a gross weight of 1660 Ibs. Their net weight
after washing was 1350 lbs. On 4 May they received ten sacks of Spanish wool
weighing 1450 lbs. gross before washing, and 1150 Ibs. net after washing. On 5
August nine sacks of Spanish wool with a gross weight of 1235 Ibs. were sent to be
washed. Their net weight after washing was 1010 lbs.

The Spanish wool sent to be washed is described as being of several qualities
(di più sorte) without any further classification, but the native wool is divided into
three grades—fine, second, and coarse. On 1 October, Giunta and Co. received four
sacks of fine Italian wool from wethers (castroni), five sacks of second grade, and two
of coarse wool, totaling 1485 Ibs. gross in weight before washing and 1150 lbs. net
after washing.

The fifth lot was of Spanish wool—seven sacks with a weight of 945 Ibs. before
washing and 770 lbs. afterwards. It was given out to be washed the same day as the
Italian wool, 1 October 1556.

Between 1 October and the following June no wool was given out to be washed
by Francesco de’ Medici and Co. either to Giunta and Co. or to any other wool-
washers. On 30 June 1557 the last lot recorded in the special journal was sent to
Giunta and Co. It consisted of eleven sacks of native ewe wool from Valdarno and
Cortona, near Florence—six sacks of fine grade, four of second, and one of coarse
wool, with a total gross weight of 1456 lbs., reduced to 1200 Ibs. after washing.

358 Ibs. of alum were used for the cleansing of the six lots of wool. Just how
alum was used in the washing process, is not clear from the documents.

APPENDIX VII

CAPODIECI IN THE FLORENTINE WOOLEN INDUSTRY

In the sixteenth-century wage ledgers of the Selfridge Collection of Medici MSS
there are accounts with numerous wool factors: factors for carding wool (fattori di
cardo); for combing it (fattori di pettine); for giving it out to be spun (Janini, stamai-
uoli); and a factor whose name, capodieci, gives no clue to his activity, but who had
charge of the cleansing and beating of wool after it came from the wool-washers.
Whether the capodieci was ever a foreman in charge of exactly ten workmen, as the
name implies, is not clear from any available documents. Nor is it clear whether the
men to whom he gave out the wool to be cleansed worked in a central workshop
belonging to the firm of Medici wool-manufacturers, or worked in their own homes.
Usually wool was cleaned, beaten, combed, and carded in the central workshop of an
industrial entrepreneur, and then sent out to be spun. There is no evidence in the
Medici documents to show that any step in the woolen industry besides the sorting
of the wool—which arrived in sacks and bales from various parts of Europe—was
carried out in a central workshop. What meager evidence there is in these account
books points rather towards a greater prevalence of the dependent wholesale handi-
craft system (the use of numerous factors serving as intermediaries between the
entrepreneur and small masters working at home) than is generally supposed to have
been true of the Florentine woolen industry in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

In the only extant special journal for dyers and workmen (libro tintori e lavor-
anti), MS 567 (7), there is one page of accounts with Batista di Pasquino, capodieci,
for Francesco de’ Medici and Company, wool-manufacturers, for 1556-1557. In
these accounts, reproduced below, we find that the capodieci was paid from eight
denari to one soldo eight denari per pound for the wool which he received to be
cleansed. Nothing is said about wages paid out by the capodieci to the men who
worked on the wool. The wool after being cleaned and beaten (and apparently
combed) was returned in faldelle (quantities of ten pounds). Why the capodieci, as
well as the factor for the combing of wool, had charge of some combing is not clear.
The detailed accounts for wool given out to the factors for combing and carding are
missing from MS 567 (7), so that no comparison with these can be made.

Following are a few entries from the detailed account in the special journal
regarding 6,273 pounds of wool handled by Batista di Pasquino during 1556-1557.
I have reproduced the credit side of his account in the special wage ledger, MS 567
(11), to which the account from the journal was posted. The debit side, which is not
given here, shows that the capodieci received the money due him in small cash pay-
ments, varying from six to twenty-one lire at a time, and usually paid out weekly.

APPENDIX VIII

SPINNING IN THE FLORENTINE WOOLEN INDUSTRY: LANINO
AND STAMAIUOLO

In the Selfridge Collection of Medici Manuscripts there are two volumes
devoted to accounts for the spinning of wool into yarn. The older account book is
the Libro di filatori (book of spinners) of the partnership entitled “Giuliano di
Rafaello de’ Medici and Co.,” Wool-Manufacturers) with accounts running from
1552 to 1556. The second book is a continuation of the first, kept by the same clerk
or bookkeeper from 1556 to 1558, for the firm under a changed name, “Francesco di
Giuliano di Rafaello de’ Medici and Co.,”’ Francesco having succeeded his father as
the major partner.

In both books there are two sets of accounts: one with Tommaso Brandolini,
lanino, who took charge of the spinning of all carded wool (Jana) for the company;
and one with the stamaiuoli (at first, during 1552 and 1553, only one in number, later,
1555-1557, increased to four), to whom the combed wool (stame) was turned over for
spinning into worsted yarn.

These volumes, folios in size, are special journals from which summary accounts
are posted to the general ledger. The accounts of wool given out to the stamaiuoli
and of the return of the yarn are kept on the left-hand pages, the accounts of wool
given to the /anino, on the right-hand.

The wool given out to be spun was designated for different kinds of cloth.
The heading running across the top of two pages names the kind of cloth to be woven
from the wool listed below. The left-hand page gives the account of the combed
wool (stame) required for the specified kind of cloth. On the right-hand page is the
account of the carded wool for the same cloth. During the Middle Ages and the
Renaissance, cloth was rarely woven entirely of carded wool, as is frequently the
case today, but usually had a warp of worsted yarn spun from combed wool and a
weft of yarn from carded wool. Hence the important distinction between stame
(combed wool and worsted yarn) and Jana (carded wool and yarn) and between the
stamaiuolo, the man who gave out combed wool to be spun, and the /anino, the man
who gave out carded wool to be spun. The combed wool was spun into yarn from a
distaff, the carded wool was spun on a spinning-wheel.

The stame for a given kind of cloth was usually intrusted to one, sometimes to
two stamaiuoli. It was not usually given out all at once but, if our documents are
typical, in two to four lots. It was returned in the form of warp yarn in small quan-
tities over a period varying from one to six months. If enough wool was being spun
for several pieces of the same kind of cloth, the warping and weaving could be begun
before all of a certain kind of yarn was returned. (Since the books of weavers,
corresponding to the two books of spinners, are missing, no study can be made of the
length of time required from the spinning of yarn to the finished weaving of a piece

of cloth.)
413

414 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

The combed wool, when given out to be spun, was in the form of bundles
(mazzi) already wound upon the distaff or ready to be wound. Each mazzo weighed
from one to one and a half pounds. The mazzi, or skeins of yarn, which were re-
turned to the entrepreneur, might be the same number as the samaiuolo received, or
a larger or smaller number. The total weight of the yarn was always less than that
of the combed wool because of a loss of about one.ounce per pound in spinning.

On the right-hand page, opposite the stamaiuolo accounts, are the accounts
with the Janino, Tommaso Brandolini, for the carded wool needed for the weft yarn
of the specified cloth. More yarn was required for the weft of a piece of cloth, one
and one-half to three times as much as was required for the warp. Hence we find
that Brandolini, the Janino for the Medici firm, frequently received more than twice
as many pounds of carded wool as the stamaiuolo received of combed wool for the
cloth.

The lanino accounts differ considerably from the stamaiuolo accounts. Where-
as on the pages devoted to the stamaiuoli only the amounts of wool given out and the
quantities returned as yarn, including the dates of receipt and return, are recorded
with the total sum in lire to be paid to the stamaiuolo for the amount of worsted yarn
he has had spun, on the /anino pages all the women spinners to whom the carded wool
is allotted are listed, with the number of bundles of wool and their weight which each
spinner received. The only dates given are those when the spinners received the
wool. There is no record of when the Janino returned it to the Medici. Only the
diagonal strokes through the lario accounts (the strokes are not found on the
left-hand pages) show that all the wool recorded on each page has been returned.
At the bottom of the page or pages (the carded wool accounts sometimes require two
pages corresponding to one for the combed wool because of the long list of spinners)
the sum to be paid to the Janino is given in lire. This sum includes the wages to be
paid to the spinners by the /anino, and does not include the extra, but customary, com-
mission given to /anini (but not to stamaiuoli) and figured up at the end of the book.
The commission paid to Brandolini was s.18 per thousand pounds of carded wool.

The names of the spinners tell us very little, except that they were all women
and lived in the country near Florence, some as far away as Fiesole and Trespiano.
Their names were evidently written in the account books by Tommaso Brandolini
himself, because they are in an entirely different, less schooled, and less legible hand
than entries in the other parts of the two books.

The relative importance of the stamaiuoli and lanini may be judged by the
much larger fee or commission received by the stamaiuoli, per pound, of the wool
which they received from the entrepreneurs and gave out to be spun, and by the
greater emphasis placed upon the stamaiuoli in sixteenth-century Florentine legal
provisions concerning the two groups.

The question of the relative dependence of the two workmen is not easy to
solve. The emphasis in the laws on regulations concerning the stamaiuoli may
signify that they retained a certain amount of industrial independence, whereas the
lanini were really employees, wholly dependent on their entrepreneur employers.
The extra commission given to lanini appears to contradict this view, but the Medici
account books seem to support it, because in the two books of spinners we find only

SPINNING IN WOOLEN INDUSTRY 415

one Zanino, who evidently devoted all his time to carrying wool back and forth
between the Medici shop and the spinners in the country. His position would
probably correspond to that of a factor in rank, but he would be very definitely an
employee, even though his salary was in the form of a percentage based on the num-
ber of pounds of yarn he brought back from the spinners.

The stamaiuoli appear to have had more freedom. In the first place the fact
that the services of more than one stamaiuolo were employed to do less work than
did the /anino, and the fact that in some years very little wool was given to certain
of the four stamaiuoli, suggests that they may have been free to work as agents or
intermediaries for more than one entrepreneur (even though the term nostro stamia-
uolo (our stamaiuolo) is used throughout the Medici account books) giving them
therefore more independence than had the Janino, who worked for only one entre-
preneur. Secondly, they did not have to give the Medici a record of the spinners
they employed, though they themselves were required by law to keep such a record,
with the amounts of wool given out to the spinners and the wages due them. Thirdly
they were examined and approved by a magistrate of the Grand Duke, which sug-
gests that their rdle in the woolen industry was considered important.

are accounts for corresponding stame and lana on pages facing each other ; the others
are the final accounts of sums due Alessandro da Berzighella, stamaiuolo, and Tom-
maso Brandolini, lanino.

APPENDIX IX

WARPERS AND WEAVERS IN THE FLORENTINE WOOLEN
INDUSTRY

After the spinning of wool into yarn, the next step in the manufacture of cloth
is warping, i.e., the measuring off of the correct number of warp threads of a specified
length to form the warp or web of a piece of cloth. For the warp only worsted yarn
(stame) was used during the Middle Ages. After the warp was properly measured,
the yarn was fastened together in loops in such a fashion that it would not become
tangled and could easily be unwound again. Then it was sized and dried. After
sizing the warp was wound upon a warp-beam, which was placed in the loom upon
which the cloth was to be woven. Next the threads were drawn through the eyes of
the heddles and the interstices of the reed and the ends of the warp were fastened to
the cloth roll at the front of the loom. The warp was then ready for weaving.

In Northern Europe (England and Flanders) warping was usually done by the
weaver; sizing was done by the weaver, or more frequently, in Flanders, by a separate
group of artisans, the sizers, who applied the dressing paste to the warp in their own
homes, and after drying the yarn returned it to the weavers, who arranged it on the
loom.

In Italy and especially in Florence, there was greater industrial specialization
than in Northern Europe during the Middle Ages. Warping was not done by the
weaver, but by a separate group, men and women warpers (orditori and orditrici) who
worked in the central workshop of an entrepreneur or in their own homes. They
usually applied the sizing to the warp which they had prepared. The laying of the
warp on the loom was done by the weaver.

Among the Medici volumes of the Selfridge Collection is one account book
devoted to warping and weaving. It is MS 560 (5) a special journal entitled “Book
of the Weavers of Garbo Cloth” (Libro de’ tessitori di Garbo), belonging to the part-
nership of Giuliano di Raffaello de’ Medici and Company, Wool-Manufacturers.
The accounts run from April 1548 to October 1551.

On the left-hand side of each double page are the records of worsted yarn given
out to women warpers (orditrici) to be warped. On the right-hand side are the
accounts of the weaving of the pieces of cloth from the warp described on the opposite
page. The heading running across the two pages names the kind of cloth to be
woven and the wool from which it is made.

For example, the first entries in the book (foll. 0”, 1") are as follows:

Twenty-nine pieces of cloth were woven from this one lot of wool. The
accounts concerning it extend over four folios. In each instance the items regarding
the preparation of the warp and the weaving of the cloth are directly opposite each
other, as shown above.

During the period of 33 years covered by this special journal, 309 pieces of
cloth were woven—100 during the first year, 75 the second year, 120 the third, and
14 cloths between May and October 1551. Most of these were of regulation length.
A few short cloths (scampoli) were woven from the remainder of certain lots of yarn.

According to the sixteenth-century Medici account books in the Selfridge
Collection, the two cloths most frequently manufactured by the Garbo manu-
facturers, i.e., those using wools other than English, were rasce and perpignani.
Today rascia means a coarse serge, but in the sixteenth century it was apparently a
fine woolen cloth, without any nap, or with a very closely sheared one, used especially
for men’s clothing, and was the most expensive Garbo cloth manufactured in the six-
teenth century. In England it was called “rash.” Perpignan cloth, an imitation of
a kind of cloth originally made in Perpignan, which appears to have been an elastic
cloth resembling our jersey, was used principally for men’s hose, and was sold at
retail for a medium price in Florence by the hosiers, not the drapers.

The accounts for the weaving of different kinds of cloth in the Book of Weavers
support the statement that a great deal of rash was woven in Florence. Over one-
third of the total output for the 34-year period, that is, 118 pieces, were rashes. All
of these, except one lot made of blue yarn, were undyed. But perpignan cloth was
not produced in as large quantities by the Medici during the period of this account
book, as it was a few years later, according to other account books in the series.
Only 24 panni perpignani are recorded in this book.

The cloth which ranked second to the rash in the number of pieces woven be-
tween 1548 and 1551 is accordellato, a ribbed cloth, coarser and wider than rash,
requiring three times as many pounds of weft yarn as of warp yarn (the usual ratio
for rash was one and one-half times as many pounds of weft as of warp yarn).
Seventy-five pieces of cloth, almost one-fourth of the total output, were accordellati,
some woven of sky-blue yarn and others of sbiadato, a pale, drab color. Pieces
woven of sbiadato yarn were frequently dyed another color in the cloth.

Eighteen pieces of say (sai), a fine serge, almost as costly as rascia, were woven.
The other cloths recorded in the book are classified according to color alone (the color

WARPERS AND WEAVERS 421

of the dye giving some clue to the fineness of the cloth), or sometimes according to the
number of heddle-harness used on the loom. For example, there are several four-
harness cloths (panno alla piana), meaning cloths with a fairly complicated twill
pattern. These latter are coarse, wide cloths, requiring almost as much weft yarn
as the accordellati. For a cloth of 60 to 65 braccia in length, the weavers received
only 10 to 12 lire, in contrast to 54 lire for a rash of the same length and three-fourths
the width.

The 309 pieces of cloth were woven by 54 weavers, all of them working at home
and apparently all in the city, not in the country. Seven of these were women, only
one of whom appears to be related to one of the male weavers, being evidently either
his wife or daughter. Most of these artisans wove less than 8 cloths for the firm
during the 3 years. Eighteen (4 of them women) wove only one cloth apiece. Five
wove 19 to 24 cloths and one wove 37 cloths. These last-mentioned weavers prob-
ably worked full time for the Medici, but the small number of cloths woven for the
firm by most of the weavers leads one to conclude that a greater number of them were
working for more than one entrepreneur. It took from 2 weeks to 2 months to weave
a cloth—depending upon the quality and length of the cloth and the skill of the
weaver—the average time being about one month. The weavers employed by the
Medici did not specialize in the weaving of a certain kind of cloth, because all of
those who wove a number of cloths included some of each kind that the company
was producing—rasce, saie, accordellati, perpignani, etc.

Some of the weavers had more than one loom. The records show that a weaver
occasionally received more than one warp at a time and returned the pieces of woven
cloth at the same, or at approximately the same time. The weaver who is credited
with 37 cloths, made 21 of them in one year, evidently by keeping two looms going.
The second loom may have been worked by his wife or by an assistant or apprentice.
In the account book only the master weavers are mentioned. The presence of
assistants in the weavers’ homes may explain why many of the weavers prepared the
cheaper as well as the more expensive cloths, entrusting to their assistants the coarser
fabrics, which required less skill in weaving. In this connection it is interesting to
note that when the above-mentioned weaver of 37 cloths received more than one warp
at a time one was usually a rascia and the other was material for a coarser cloth.

The accounts of the individual weavers are kept in the rear of the volume on
folios 160 to 165. No amounts are deducted from the sums due to the weavers for
weaving cloth for advances, or loans made on looms. Loans to weavers on their
looms, or the purchase and selling of the weavers’ looms by the industrial entre-
preneurs, were strictly prohibited by an ordinance of 1546. This was repealed in
1560 on the ground that it was causing hardship to the weavers. Whether the letter
of the law was obeyed by the Medici wool-merchants between 1546 and 1560, or
whether such transactions were merely kept out of their books, cannot be answered
from the material at hand.

The weavers were paid on either of two bases, either so much per piece of cloth
of a given kind regardless of length (provided the cloth did not fall short of the mini-
mum required length). For example, the weavers received 1.25 for each blue
accordellato, 1.24 for each grey, i.e., undyed, perpignano, 1.10 for each panno isbiadato

422 APPENDICES ON TERMS AND PRACTICES

or turchino, etc.; or so much per braccio or passino of woven cloth. For example, the
rate for says was 1.4 per passino, for grey rash 1.5 per passino and for blue rash 1.1 per
braccio.

All of these rates correspond to those prescribed by an ordinance of 1 March
1545/46. There is only one group of prices for weavers which is not fully covered
by the ordinance and which presents a puzzling problem. Thirty-six cloths of panni
bianchi sopramani alla piana (undyed four-harness superfine (?) cloth) were woven.
About half of them had warps of 9 passini and 50 paiuole (50 X 40 = 2,000 warp
threads), and more than twice as many pounds of weft as warp yarn, and when
woven measured 60 to 62 braccia. For these the weavers received only 10 lire per
cloth. But for the other half, which had warps of 11 passini and 70 paiuole (70 X
40 = 2,800 warp threads), the same proportion of weft and warp yarn, and which
measured 72 to 78 braccia when finished, they received 24 lire per cloth. The
ordinance prescribed 24 lire for the 11 passini cloth, but failed to list the 9 passini
length. Why more than twice as much was paid for a cloth only to + longer and
with only 2 more warp threads is not at all clear.

In contrast to the large number of weavers to whom work was given out by this
partnership, only 5 warpers, all women, were employed to prepare the 309 warps.
They took from 5 to 15 days, usually about one week, to prepare a warp. All of
these warpers probably worked at home, though men warpers sometimes worked in
a central workshop. Two kinds of warp-frames were then in use: one which could
be fastened to the wall, and the other, composed of four vertical uprights and many
horizontal pegs, which could stand in any open space.

The piece wages for the warpers according to the Medici accounts were: 1355
for a rascia warp of nine passini and 110 paiuole; 1.2 s.5 for a say warp of 11 passini;
1.1 s.15 for each warp of accordellati, perpignani, and panni larghi; and 1.1 for the
other panni.

There are no references to sizing in this volume. The women warpers were
apparently paid only for warping, but the price of warping may have included sizing.
Or the sizing may have been done by the weaver and included in the price of weaving.
It could not have been done in the central workshop of the Medici after the warp was
returned to the bottega because the warp was frequently given to the weaver the same
day that it was returned by the warper.
